# **PREFACE** 

Copper 2013 International Conference is the 8<sup>th</sup> version of the most important global meeting that brings together leading scientists, researchers, academics, and executives from different companies and organizations devoted to the areas of economy, copper processing, metallurgical extraction techniques; environmental compatibility; copper applications, copper recovery, and waste management and recycling techniques. At the same time, the challenges faced by different mining projects will be addressed. We appreciate the work and collaboration from colleagues coming from over 30 countries and representing more than 300 companies and institutions. 

Copper 2013 Conferences find their origin in the joint work conducted between the Chilean Institute of Mining Engineers (IIMCh) and the Metallurgical Society of the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum (METSOC). Since 2007, when the Copper Conference was held in Toronto, new co-organizer institutions have helped disseminate the results achieved by the Conferences while granting these a strong global character in terms of convening power, submittal of papers, and the generation of collaborative knowledge. We deeply appreciate the disinterested contribution from GDMB of Germany, MMIJ of Japan, and TMS and SME from USA. 

This time, the current global situation is not only a scenario where competitive prices are being realized but also where strong and serious uncertainties are being handled in connection with the global economy; energy and key resources prices. 

Globally, ore grades have declined to historically low levels and, therefore, the recycling and recovery of what used to be waste material, nowadays represent great opportunities for the overall development of new projects. Water uses in production processes and the solutions applied no doubt represent a source of knowledge for the community gathered at this venue. Likewise, new long-term and mid-term forecasts to be made in the future will certainly set their focus on eventual challenges and on mining and metallurgical development opportunities in the decades ahead. 

The total of 330 papers submitted in response to the original call will present the main changes to take place in metallurgical processes, as well as the state-of-theart techniques responsible for providing effective solutions to new challenges posed by metallurgical processes. The widespread interest generated by innovations, particularly in the area of pyrometallurgy will undoubtedly occupy a special place in the course of the Conference, thanks to the research and development of technological solutions conducted in countries like China, for example.

Copper 2013 Organizing Committee. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ ### **FOREWORD** For the first time since the Copper-Cobre Conferences started more than 25 years ago, for 2013 a symposium was planned to deal with subjects related to the first stages of the copper life cycle: under the heading of “Aspects of Geo Metallurgical Challenges of Mining Projects”, authors were invited to propose papers on topics like geometallurgical modeling, integrated mine design and mine planning, nontraditional pre concentration and alternative processes towards energy and water optimization, and challenges and alternative designs towards massive open pit and underground operations in the copper industry. The response from the professional community was very encouraging. Authors who work in mining companies, consulting groups, equipment manufacturing, universities and other organizations submitted more than 30 abstracts to this symposium. The papers which were approved for the Conference are published in this volume in the same order in which they were scheduled to be presented. The most numerous group of papers deals with aspects of geometallurgy. The fundamentals of this “art and science” have been around for ages, since certainly the gaining of metals from ores is only possible because every geological species or mineral delivers particular responses when exposed to water, heat and other chemical or physical metallurgical processes. What has been relatively new is the definition of Geometallurgy as a distinct discipline which formalizes the relationships between geology, mine planning, ore processing and extractive metallurgy with the purpose of building a common and consistent body of knowledge which allows to better understand and optimize the chain linking the successive unit operations which transform a “geological anomaly” (the deposit) into ingots of pure metal. Papers were received mainly from Chile, the host country, but as well from the United States, Japan, Germany and Australia. Many are related to specific operations and convey a represe

ntative picture on how the Chilean copper industry is facing different aspects related to the planning process around the particular variations of the behavior of ores when they are subject to treatment. Others are more general in nature and deal with some fundamental issues of geometallurgy. 

We hope that those readers who attended the Copper 2013 Conference will enjoy revisiting the papers which attracted most their attention, but that this volume will prove useful as well as source of reference and information for other operators, researchers and consultants in copper mining who could not make it to Santiago in early December 2013. May this volume trigger innovative ideas to face the difficulties which will continue challenging our industry in the future.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

Caserones Project is the Copper and Molybdenum mining project in Chile managed by SCM Minera Lumina Copper Chile (MLCC).  This project is owned 100% by Japanese companies, Pan Pacific Copper Co., Ltd. (66% owned by JX Nippon Mining and Metals Corporation and 34% by Mitsui Mining & Smelting Co., Ltd.) with 75% and Mitsui & Co., Ltd. with 25%. 

Since acquiring the mining concession in May 2006, various stages of study have been conducted based on the data obtained in exploratory drilling, metallurgical tests, and other researches.  The result of the study showed that Caserones Project is economically and technically feasible and the environmental approval for developing the project was granted by Environmental Committee of Region `Ⅲ` of Chile.  Accordingly, this lead the Company to decide advancing the Caserones Project into construction stage in February 2010.  The construction began in March 2010, and the operation commences in 2013. 

The Caserones copper and molybdenum deposits(“Caserones deposits”) are located in the municipal district of Tierra Amarrilla, 162 km southeast from the city of Copiapo, the capital of Region `Ⅲ` of Chile. There are mining projects in operation and under development near the Caserones deposits. Figure 1 shows the location of Caserones deposits.

## **DESCRIPTION OF THE PROJECT** 

## **Geology and Operation** 

## <u>Geology and Deposits</u> 

Caserones deposits are copper-molybdenum porphyry copper deposits which locate in the southern edge of the Maricunga belt.  The geology of this area consists mainly of the Miocene dacite porphyry intruded in the Palezoic monzogranite and the igneous breccia.  Dominant alteration is potassic alteration and its overprinting phyllic alteration, while propylite alteration is stronger at the margin of deposits. 

From above, deposits consist of leaching zone, oxide ore zone, secondary sulfide zone and primary sulfide zone.  The main oxide copper mineral is chalcanthite, accompanying chrysocolla and brochantite.  The majority of the oxide copper mineral generates in fracture filling.  The copper mineral of the secondary sulfide zone is mainly 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

7 

chalcocite, with a few covellite.  The copper mineral of the primary sulfide zone is mainly chalcopyrite with trace bornite. 

## <u>Mining Operation</u> 

The ore is extracted by open pit mining at large scale, including 1.05 billion tons(average CuT 0.34%) of sulfide ore for flotation and 0.30 billion tons(average CuT 0.25%) of oxide, low-grade sulfide and mixed ore for Dump leach and SX-EW. 

Mining is operated in a conventional large scale open pit metode using blasthole drills, an electric shovel, a hydraulic shovel, large loaders and 300-tonne haul trucks.  Ore for flotation process is carried to the primary crusher plant to the south of the pit.  On the other hand, run-of mine ore for SX-EW is dumped on the leaching pad in Caserones Valley, which is near the pit to the east.  Waste is sent to the waste dump located to the northwest of the pit. The planned mine life stripping ratio is 0.5. 

## <u>Flotation</u> 

The concentrator plant is located to the south of the pit, in which copper and molybdenum concentrate are produced by flotation.  Ore from the mine is directly dumped into the throat of a gyratory crusher (60"x113").  Crushed product is carried to a coarse mineral stockpile by a downhill conveyor.  The ore withdrawn from the mineral stockpile is processed in the grinding section which consists of a large SAG mill which is 40 feet in diameter by 26 feet long, two ball mills which are 27 feet in diameter by 46 feet long, and pebble crushers.  The grinding product is sent to the copper-molybdenum flotation section, where the ore i

s separated into copper-molybdenum bulk concentrate and tailings.  The copper-molybdenum bulk concentrate is processed to produce copper concentrate and molybdenum concentrate by selective flotation.  These concentrates are filtered at the same site and transported by trucks. 

The tailings handling is designed to minimize water consumption by depositing coarse fraction (sand) and fine fraction (slime) of tailing separately.  The tailings are fed to hydrocyclones by gravity, and the underflow, sand, is disposed in the sand deposit 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

8 

adjacent to the concentrator.  The overflow, slime, is thickened by high density thickeners and the thickened slime is transported to the slime dam by gravity flow located approximately 10km away from the concentrator.  Recovered water from both tailings facilities is recycled back to the concentrator plant. The nominal capacity of the concentrator is to process 105,000 tonnes of ore per day. 

## <u>Dump leach and SX-EW</u> 

Ore to be processed at leaching is transported by mine trucks and dumped filling the valley near the mine pit.  Because of steep topography of the project area, the ore is stacked on a permanent leach pad sequentially in several lifts of 20 meters high for first lifts followed by 40 meters lifts for the remaining lifts.  Dilute sulfuric acid is sprayed through drip emitters on the ore piled in the leaching pad lined with geomembrane so as to prevent seepage of the solution out of the process system.  The irrigation surface is covered with a thin plastic film in order to limit water consumption by evaporation, control heat losses and prevent freezing. 

Pregnant Leach Solution `（` PLS `）` from the leaching pad is sent to SX-EW plant to recover the copper in the solution.  The SX plant consists of extraction (three stages), stripping (one stage) and washing (one stage).  The strip solution is processed at the EW plant which has 60 EW cells, to deposit copper cathode on stainless steel permanent cathodes.  The nominal capacity of the EW plant is 30,000 tonnes of cathode per year.

## **Geometallurgical Model for the Production Plan** 

During the development of the project the geological information and results of metallurgical tests were studied to find out the geological parameters which affect to metallurgical performance such as recovery, ore hardness and concentrate grade.  The geometallurgical model of the project was prepared with the parameters identified in the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

10 

study. 

For example, a matrix of geological parameters which consist of 3 types of lithology by 3 alteration by 3 mineralogy was investigated to extract parameters which affect copper recovery in the flotation.  As the result of the investigation it was found that chemical composit

ion, proportion of CuAC to CuT affects stronger than copper mineralogy on the copper recovery. In addition, flotation behavior of the material of MZG and BX lithology is similar, while PDA has different characteristic from them. CuAC and CuT is determined by chemical assay, which is CuAC is citric acid soluble Cu and CuT is total Cu. The matrix for the investigation is shown in Table 1. 

Table 1-Matrix of geological parameters 

|**Lithology**|**Alteration**|**Mineralogy**|
|---|---|---|
|MZG(Monzogranite)|QS(Quartz Sericite)|SS(SS>65%)|
|BX(Breccia)|KF(K-Feldespar)|SS+PS(65%>=SS>=35%)|
|PDA(Dacitic Porphyry)|CL(Clorite)|PS(35%>SS)|



* SS: Secondary Sulfide   PS:Primary Sulfide 

Therefore, chemical composition and lithology are defined as parameters to estimate the recovery, where lithology is grouped into 2, MZG+BX and PDA, which were initially 3, MZG, BX and PDA.  Then equations which estimate copper recovery with geological information were determined to put recovery into each block of the deposit.

As the same way principal metallurgical parameters such as concentrate grade and ore hardness were correlated with geological parameters to form the geometallurgical model.  Then the obtained data is put into each block.  The production plan was elaborated by the information of the blocks put in and operation conditions to optimize the economic benefit of the project.

## **Initiatives toward the Local Community** 

As a part of sustainability activity, MLCC has carried the Community Management Program into action, which consists of three principal pillars.  These are “Water management” which is essential for the dry area of northern Chile, “Road safety” from the mine to the port, and “Regional employment” which encourages the development of the local community. 

## <u>Water management</u>

## **ABSTRACT** 

The South American copper industry is facing infrastructure constraints in two major ways; the cost and lead time of new or expanded facilities and insufficient supply of electrical power. Infrastructure now represents over 75% of a green field project’s capital cost having increased from around 50% a decade ago. The demand for electrical power continues to increase in proportion to copper output; however investment in power generation lags behind the potential copper production growth rate. 

Opportunities exist to overcome local power constraints. Learning’s from the aggressive expansion of South Africa’s platinum industry last decade can be applied to the South American copper industry. Platinum production in one company was doubled with only a small increase in total power consumption by assessing the complete mine to metal supply chain. 

Now infrastructure is the largest project cost it seems logical to include it in the geometallurgy design or optimisation phase. i-GeoMet<sup>TM</sup> does exactly this with the aim of building smaller and staged infrastructure optimised to each specific mining project. ## **INTRODUCTION** 

Global ore grades continue to decrease and mines continue to get larger, fuelling the need for more enabling infrastructure across the pit to port chain. Capital and operating costs are increasing; particularly power, water and labour. Prior to 2004 the cost of plant, equipment and machinery in mining projects represented the majority of capital costs. Since then however, infrastructure costs have soared to represent over 75% of the total project cost, as illustrated in Figure 1 (ABS, 2011). Responding to this industry shift requires an improved mine development approach linking infrastructure to geometallurgy. Given the cost and complexity of infrastructure – particularly in developing economies – Owners need to prioritise the design and construction of complex infrastructure and integrate this approach into the development of the mining and processing designs.

The success of the next generation of mining projects relies on the management of infrastructure cost and risk. Still today many projects use feasibility techniques developed late last century that centred on the processing plant and mine as parallel designs; associated infrastructure took a back seat. It was assumed that any infrastructure could be delivered along the way. This approach was suitable when infrastructure was a minor risk and cost consideration. 

Green field mining projects attempt to align with commodity price cycles. The primary commodity boom in the past decade has demonstrated how power and transport infrastructure can make – or break – the economics of mining projects whether in

## **GLOBAL CONTEXT** 

Average ore grades have halved over the last 30 years (Prior 2011, CRC ORE 2012). During this period both the annual production and reserves of all minerals have increased significantly (Mudd 2010, Schodde 2010). Using copper as an example, from 1990 to 2010, global reserves have increased approximately 100 per cent to 550 Mt, while the production grade has decreased approximately 30 per cent (from 1.5 per cent to 1 per cent Cu). The discovery grade has been static and significantly below current operating grades (0.5 - 0.6 per cent Cu) (Schodde 2010). Hence, the majority of the increase in the reserve base has occurred via a reduction in cut-off grades (due to technology driving throughput up and unit costs down) rather than the discovery/replacement of deposits. Synonymous with accessing high value ore early in the life of a single mine, the industry as a whole has logically accessed the simpler, lower cost and higher grade mines first. As these become depleted the mining industry has been searching and developing mines further from the market, in less developed geographies and with lower ore grades. Over the next 10 - 15 years production grades are forecast to continue declining by 15 – 25 per cent (Figure 3). In parallel ore body complexity will soar (in terms of grade and processing variability), the abundance of deleterious elements will increase (particularly arsenic and fluorine) and the depth of mining will all put upward pressure on operating costs. These trends suggest upward C1 cost and project risk movements.

Common risks include a lack of enabling infrastructure (power, water, transport, accommodation), availability of a local skilled workforce and exposure to corruption, security and other geopolitical threats. This is also emerging for copper in South America where decreasing ore grade and increasing throughput scale are driving the need for more productive ore and product transport solutions. As the mine export and supply import logistics chains lengthen, they become more complex with a likelihood of traversing difficult terrain, multiple international borders and often primitive or hostile communities. This means existing logistics ‘rules of thumb’ around the optimum balance between capital and operating costs for maximum NPV, or minimum life of mine cost, have limited applicability. Historically, the approach has been to achieve regulatory compliance, especially for environmental and social impact. The new South African Mining Charter is indicative of a rising global trend to make such compliance more stringent, particularly regarding community development. ## **IMPACT OF GLOBAL TRENDS** 

The impact of global trends will continue to place new challenges on the mining industry. Traditional methodologies (predicated on pre-trend conditions) are therefore not ideally suited to addressing the new challenges. In some cases this has resulted in destruction of project value. Invalid and out-dated assumptions have led to false valuations and specifically overly intensive capital expenditure. The traditional mining development approach has been one of a linear progression through exploration, geological modelling, mine planning, process design and finally infrastructure with limited feedback or iteration loops. Project value analysis has usually been a last resort to reduce costs and improve NPV at the back end of a study if the target internal tollgate return on investment is not achieved. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

22 

Traditional methodology relegates infrastructure to the tail end of the project development chain, where infrastructure designers are issued with a life of mine plan to provide the quantities and rates of power supply, water and product transportation dictated by the previous stages. This has often resulted in the ‘biggest hammer’ infrastructure solution; where the infrastructure has been sized to provide for short-term peaks in service demand with little or no regard for mine design, geometallurgy or step changes in the cost of infrastructure along the quantity/rate increase curve. For example, power stations may be designed to match peak demand from the mining and p

rocessing design in a single project year only. The mining and processing has, in such a case, been scheduled and designed to achieve a nominal optimum NPV from early mining and processing of the maximum amount of the highest grade ore. This decision was made without full regard to the hardness and energy input characteristics requiring a power supply far in excess of that which was required for the remainder of the life of mine. 

Unfortunately large mining projects have become synonymous with schedule delays (Figure 7), the impacts of which are to delay product to market, postpone income and therefore significantly reduce NPV and project value. Today a mining project has less to do with tonnes and grade but rather sustainability and risk. Figure 7 indicates that sustainability issues were the most prominent cause identified for delays in a Goldman Sachs 2011 survey of 190 projects. These issues relate to community consultation, social licence and government approvals. The larger the proposed scale and footprint – throughput, geographical, logistical, environmental, governmental and social – the more complex and challenging these sustainability aspects become and the higher the risk of time and value delays. 



Figure 7 – Causes of project delays from a survey of 190 delayed projects (Xstrata 2012. Source: Goldman Sachs) 

One industry response to poor project performance has been to invest more in front end studies to lower risk and uncertainty surrounding the increasingly complex

sustainability and technical issues. The benefits of this front-end loading (FEL) approach have been well documented over many years. The ability to influence overall project costs and make design changes in early study stages, at comparatively low cost relative to the total project investment, is a long established principle. Notwithstanding this, some Owners have sought to shave further money out of the project development cost through use of standardised designs. An approach based on the concept that each installation of a process plant and surrounding ore handling infrastructure does not need to be fully redesigned each time. In reality, the combination of project-to-project ore variability, geography, operator skills and infrastructure scale/complexity has meant that such savings have proved to be illusory. Often the hours associated with engineering design and drafting re-work to fit a standard design to each scenario is greater than designing from scratch. A case study illustrating the value destroyed by using this approach is included in this paper.

## **CONCLUSION** 

A major challenge facing the Chilean copper industry is energy supply because the provision of infrastructure may limit the rate of new mine establishment or expansion of existing operations. The energy demands of copper mines are dominated by transport (fuel for mining equipment and product transport) and processing (electricity for concentrators, smelters and refineries). 

i-GeoMet<sup>TM</sup> is an integrated approach to mine project development that considers the entire supply and value chain from geology, mining, processing, water supply, product transport and enabling infrastructure. By using a fully integrated approach the design of infrastructure can be optimised to minimise the scale of equipment, facilities and therefore energy consumption to provide a fully optimised life of mine business case. Smaller infrastructure not only consumes less energy, but is faster to construct and cheaper to operate and maintain. 

JK Aurecon case studies demonstrate that an integrated approach to mine development or expansion can provide increased metal production without a proportional increase in energy demand. With mining infrastructure now representing 75 per cent of the total project capital cost, optimising these enabling facilities can provide large improvements in project risk, economics and construction schedule.

## **CASE STUDY 1 – EXPANDING METAL PRODUCTION AT A TIME OF ELECTRICITY RESTRICTIONS** 

Between 1999 and 2011, Anglo Platinum’s South African operations underwent significant expansion to take advantage of growing Platinum Group Metals (PGM) demand and upward trending metal prices. Expansion plans proposed doubling the PGM output which relied on approximately doubling the tonnage of all unit processes from mining through concentrating to smelting and refining. ROM ore capacity grew from 22 Mtpa in 1998 to 41-44 Mtpa in 2005-2007 (Rule, 2009). Part way through the expansion programme, South Africa began to suffer from inconsistent electricity supply as construction of new thermal power plants lagged behind industrial and domestic demand. Mining was the largest single consumer of electricity in South Africa and Anglo Platinum was one of the largest mining sector consumers. By 2008 Anglo Platinum consumed 1 GVA of the total 38 GVA electrical capacity in South Africa (2.6%). Nearly 40% was made up of comminution (0.195 GVA) and smelting (0.185 GVA) unit processes. Power therefore became an infrastructure constraint that had to be overcome to meet the planned PGM expansion plan. 

As it was no longer possible to expand mining and processing infrastructure (and consequent power consumption) in proportion to PGM output, a step change in efficiency was necessary. Anglo Platinum deduced that building additional power-hungry smelters was no longer the solution and looked to other parts of the supply chain to find the necessary efficiencies. Since 1999, new concentrator technologies and flow sheets had been tested with the original aim of maintaining PGM recovery in the face of decreasing mine grades and increasing complexity of mineralogy. The increasing proportion of complex UG2 and Platreef ores also led Anglo Platinum to improve their mineralogical knowledge and tie process response to their resource mod

els in a worldclass geometallurgy approach. 

The effect of different technologies and flow sheets was investigated in the concentrator plants and the application of inert mainstream stirred milling and scavenger concentrate regrinding had the most pronounced impact on grade and recovery improvement. In the face of electrical supply constraints, Anglo Platinum identified that these new technologies and flow sheets could be used in a different way than originally planned; to increase concentrate grade whilst maintaining recovery (rather than just a recovery increase). The energy impact of this approach is very significant as the higher concentrate grade results in lower concentrate mass (smelter feed) thus the energy requirement for smelting is reduced when expressed as kWh/t milled. The question asked was, would it be possible to increase concentrate grades sufficiently so the smelters could produce the expanded PGM tonnage in matte, but only treat the same input concentrate tonnage? The possibility of doing this would mean that only a minor increase in electricity consumption would be required compared to the original plan of smelting a higher tonnage of lower grade concentrates (with a proportional and massive power demand increase). It was found that this was possible and Anglo Platinum set about altering concentrator flow sheets in existing and new plants to make it so. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

29 

Somewhat paradoxically the concentrator changes required the addition of equipment (i.e. more installed power per tonne milled) to achieve higher concentrate grades. However, the overall energy consumption per tonne milled across the supply chain significantly reduced. Figure 12 shows the equivalent direct electrical power consumed in each unit process that was modified for the equivalent PGM output. The overall result was 65 % of the original power consumption per unit of PGM produced and Anglo Platinum successfully met their expansion target with only a small total power increase, in the face of a major infrastructure constraint. By not building additional smelters, operating costs were significantly reduced, as was the capital cost of expansion.

This is a way of challenging the design team to meet production targets in alternative, lower cost ways. ## **CASE STUDY 2 – THE IMPORTANCE OF PRODUCT TRANSPORT INFRASTRUCTURE** 

The transport industry in Chile is the highest energy consumer. Efficient transport of ore product to market is a fundamental requirement of a feasible and profitable mining business. As outlined previously the global trends are for these product logistics chains to lengthen, become more complex, and contribute ever increasing proportions of the cost of a mine development, both in capital and operating terms. Indeed the lack of such a logistics chain is a fatal flaw to any mine. Undersised ore logistics chain infrastructure is therefore a constraint to growth and mine planning flexibility whereas oversized infrastructure represents considerable over capitalisation. 

In this context it is somewhat surprising therefore, that the standard mining approach to product transport logistics chains is to allow the mine plan to dictate the sizing of the transport infrastructure without any design feedback loop. A common example from the most transport infrastructure intense industries, such as coal or iron ore, would be that the mine planners and process designers decide on producing 10 Mtpa every year for the life of the mine, without reference to the fact that there may be a step change in transport infrastructure cost at 9 Mtpa, or that with the same infrastructure 12 Mtpa may be readily achievable. 

In fact determining the capacity of a product logistics chain is by no means a simple exercise given the interactions between the various steps in the chain from, for example: mine product stockpile to train loading station by conveyor, rail to the port, to port stockyard by conveyor and reclaim and convey to shiploading. Each step in the chain can be optimised in isolation but in dynamic systems an optimised chain is not the same as connecting optimised links. This is further complicated when rail and port infrastructure becomes multi-user servicing many mines. 

In May 2009 the Minerals Council of Australia (MCA) published a report by ACIL Tasman on the Vision 2020 Project: The Australian Minerals Industry Path to Prosperity. The report noted that: 

_We would note that a failure to implement (or delays in implementing) some of the existing infrastructure expansion plans would lead to the anticipated growth in minerals production being constrained and actual outcomes being pushed more towards those suggested by the Holding the Line and Decline scenarios._ 

It divided Australia into 21 resource regions. Assessment of the “Key Infrastructure Gaps” for 20 of these regions listed the ore transport facilities of ports and railways, usually in the top three. 

The rapid expansion of mine development in the 2000s associated with the largely China driven boom in coal and iron ore prices saw this infrast

ructure stretched

## **CURRENT PRACTICE** 

The current industry practices to target optimal value were developed last century and focused primarily on the geology, mine and the process plant as the primary drivers of project value. ## **HOLISTIC VALUE CHAIN I-GEOMET™ APPROACH** 

The i-GeoMet™ approach, advocated by the authors, recognises the impacts of recent trends exposing limitations in the current practice, developed when the fundamental drivers of value were balanced in a significantly different way to current trends. In particular the holistic value chain approach recognises and integrates into its decision making: 

- The dominant cost of enabling infrastructure 

- The fundamental risks and opportunities associated with sustainable development incorporating environmental and community aspects 

- The more complex, variable and lower average grade ore bodies requiring more rigorous geometallurgical definition, mine planning and process design 

Figure 18 shows a flow chart of the decision approach as follows:

- Project Identification: exploration to locate and identify the resource and identify the potential project 

- Project framework parameters: establishment of the key external inputs and parameters which would define the success or failure of the project including efficiencies in items like energy and water to drive up project value and contribute to overall corporate footprint reduction and sustainability 

- Project design: an integrated approach which links all aspects of the project in determining critical mine design parameters (such as cut-off grade) and linking through the mine schedule to the process and infrastructure to optimise NPV 

- Project evaluation: assessment of whether an optimal (not necessarily optimised) business case for the deposit, infrastructure needs and sustainability factors has been achieved, not merely whether the maximum tonnes of ore have been extracted or whether a hurdle rate has been achieved. If considered sub-optimal the project is iterated starting back at the project parameters stage with these value drivers being reassessed against previous iterations.

The outcomes of the i-GeoMet<sup>TM</sup> holistic value chain approach are to increase project value through an integrated approach to the optimisation of key parameters, and reduction of project risk through better understanding of the design linkages and the sensitivity of the project to variance in the ore body geology, mineralogy and metallurgy.

FLSmidth Drive Midvale, UT 84047 Samuel.Yu@flsmidth.com_ ## **ABSTRACT** Testwork programs for greenfield projects are essential for effective process design, accurate equipment sizing and timely startups. Adequate testwork is even more imperative as currently mined ore bodies are becoming deeper, harder, finer grained, contain a more complex mineralogy and exhibit larger ore variation. Further, these ores do not always fit within the framework of currently available testwork databases and installations. The effects of inadequate testwork are evident in some of the mill sizing errors made in recent years, and many non-optimal flowsheet designs and underachieving plant performances can be traced back to the lack of quality testwork planning at the beginning of the project. Achieving an adequate testwork program is challenging. The ramifications of inadequate testwork and lack of mineralogical ore characterization on equipment sizing and process design are discussed to emphasize the importance of testwork programs and planning. Two important aspects of the testwork planning, ore sampling and the right type of testwork, are discussed. Explanations, examples, interpretation and cost estimates of testwork programs will be presented. Finally, recommendations are made for the planning, execution and utilization of a testwork program. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 44 ## **INTRODUCTION** Mineral processing testwork is a key component in the development of a mineral processing flowsheet and the subsequent design basis. The result of the testwork will not only directly impact the process design, equipment selection and sizing, products plan and specifications, but also is influential in determining whether a plant can reach the designed operating performance and acquire the

desired return on investment (ROI). 

However, there is a tendency in the industry to cut down the testwork cost and shorten the period of mineral processing testwork. Robust pilot plant testing is too often replaced by modeling or simulations. Although this appears to save time and money upfront, it often comes back to damage the project with a slow ramp-up and unsatisfactory plant performance. Some recent projects have suffered from operating below design criteria, which is often due to insufficient testwork and the absence of a full process assessment at the beginning of the project. The purposes of this paper are to provide a general approach on the typical testwork required to sufficiently design a greenfield copper processing project, and to serve as a guideline on how much and at what stage of the project the testwork should be conducted. A number of specific examples are cited with respect to both positive and negative approaches. 

Currently, there are several experienced metallurgical laboratories around the world that can conduct competent testwork services. These include SGS Lakefield, Hazen Research, Dawson Metallurgical Laboratories, Mintek, G&T Metallurgical Services, TOMS, and, of course, the internal metallurgical laboratories of some of the large mining companies. However, all these metallurgical laboratories alone are not enough to provide quality testwork for the plant design. Collaboration between the client “owner,” the EPCM company and the metallurgical laboratories is key to the success of the testwork program and subsequent plan. As indicated earlier, when proposing the testwork plan there should be a profound knowledge from all parties regarding the orebody, ore types and head grade, the ore mineralogy, ore variation, geological conditions, mining method and schedule, processing methodology, and the expected operation economics. This information can be used to assist in the sample acquisition, and selecting the right type of testwork together with right amount of testwork for the design purpose. 

## **TESTWORK PROGRAMS AND PLANNING** 

Although the testwork cost seems high as viewed by others at the beginning of any project, in fact this is not the case. It is obvious that planning the types of tests and number of tests is important, but from a high-level macro viewpoint less than several million dollars of testwork on a plus US$1 billion project can be justified. Simplistically, testwork normally costs less than 0.5% of the overall project cost. 

From another aspect, the impact on the project economics from an inaccurate test result is huge. Considering the typical case of a copper concentrator with a throughput of 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

45 

100,000 metric tons per day, assuming 0.5% copper head grade and 3.3 US$/lb, every 0.1% recovery difference corresponds to US$1.21 million per year! In practice, it is not uncommon that the plant recovery can be as much as 5% lower than the designed valu

e due to poor process design and insufficient testwork. This corresponds to a loss of US$60 million per year. Even considering the time value of the money, the initial cost of the testwork is insignificant compared to the risk of such a loss. 

For most copper concentrators, the comminution circuit is the most common bottleneck for plant throughput. Insufficient sampling, or insufficient testwork, can cause the mill sizing to be inaccurate and result in a costly lack of achieving nameplate capacity. 

As an example of the SAG mill sizing and selection, a lack of adequate testwork taking into consideration variability or ore hardness mapping can result in the mill throughput being short by up to 30% of the nameplate capacity. For a 100,000 metric ton per day copper concentrator—assuming 0.5% copper head grade and copper price of 3.3US$/lb—10% of throughput loss equals a revenue loss of US$120.5 million. 

Testwork programs and planning should be based on the orebody to be exploited, though geologists, mining engineers and metallurgists tend to have different perspectives when evaluating the orebody. It is important for a project team to get process input at the beginning of the project. For example, when the geologist and mining engineer undertake resource and reserve estimations, these are mainly based on the volume of the orebody and the ore head grade. They are seldom based on the variation of recovery, reagent considerations and final product quality caused by the ore complexity and variation, which can heavily influence the project economics, testwork plan and flowsheet design. 

A good testwork program should consider the sampling, the content and scale of testwork, the timing of testwork and budgetary constraints of the project. It should be based on the size and complexity of the orebody, the ore variation, the ore mineralogy, the process method expected, project schedule and the economic requirements. The testwork planning should start with the exploration of the deposit and include early input from the metallurgist, project manager, geologist and mining engineer. 

Though the quality of the testwork is crucial for a quality plant design and satisfactory plant operation, its importance is not always fully recognized. There is a tendency in the mining industry to take a shortcut on the testwork and initial study to minimize the front-end cost and expedite the project schedule. This is mainly due to the underestimation of the innate risks and uncertainties associated with a mining operation. The negative effects of this shortcut are often overlooked, and the impact from insufficient testwork to the quality of process design and future plant operation includes: 

- Process flowsheet design flaws—underperforming flowsheet 

- Incorrect equipment selection and sizing 

- Reduced plant throughput (lower than design) 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

46 

- Product not meeting market specification 

- Reduced recovery against desi

gn - Reduced plant availability - Slower plant commissioning and ramp-up - Expensive process modification after plant is running All these risks directly impact the potential economic return of the project. Due to insufficient testwork and resulting process design flaws, many operations experience project delays, frequent process design changes and slow plant commissioning ramp-up. Even worse, some of the plants can never make the designed plant throughput or escape from a negative cash flow scenario. This in turn jeopardizes the relationship with the financial institutions, and partially explains why many mining operations have had greater difficulty obtaining investment funding since 2008. Considering the overall picture above, the initial cost of the testwork is only a very small portion of the total project cost. Based on the test plan, bench-scale lab testing can vary from US$50,000 up to US$1.5 million. The pilot test typically runs from US$200,000 up to several millions of US$. Compared with the whole project cost, the upfront cost from testwork is typically less than 0.5% of total project CAPEX. Although a representative sample is always difficult to achieve, a good sampling plan can make the sample as close as t

o the future plant feed as possible. A good sampling plan is not only the precondition to acquire a representative sample for the testwork, but also the basis for accurate orebody estimation. Focusing on robust sampling for the first five operational years is recommended. It needs to involve multiple parties in generating a good sampling plan. This typically includes a geologist, mining engineers, a metallurgist and a mineralogist. The client, the engineering EPCM company and the testing lab should all be involved in the sampling work. It is recommended that the sample representivity should be evaluated before the testwork. The most fundamental principle for sampling is to make sure that the test sample is basically similar to the future plant feed. It must always be borne in mind that the best testwork program and the most accurate analysis will never overcome the deficiencies created by poor sampling. 

Generally, the sample should be representative of the entire orebody which is going to be mined. Multiple sampling locations should be distributed over the whole orebody and should not be too concentrated in a particular region. They should cover both the edge of the orebody and the center of the orebody. Distribution of sampling locations should also be considered in order to represent different ore types and ore grade. Mineralogy frequently changes with depth—it is typical that the upper portion of an orebody contains the oxide and transitional ore and the lower portion is primary sulphide ore. Therefore, depth should also be a factor in sampling considerations. If it is difficult to obtain sufficient samples, the samples should be at least representative of the plant feed during the first 5–10 years of operation. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

49 

Special attention should be given to rock type variation, ore boundary and high alteration of ore. The mineralogical composition, head grade, chemical components, ore texture, liberation condition of valuable minerals, content of economic byproducts and critical impurity minerals in the ore should all be considered in sampling classification. If there is a significant difference in ore characteristics between different ore types, each ore type should have its own test sample so that testwork can be conducted on each ore type and blends of different ore types. If future operations will not mine the ore separately or process the ore differently, a composite sample may be acceptable. When there are other valuable byproducts in the orebody, based on its mineralogy and geological properties, a representative sample should be taken for byproducts recovery tests. This is especially important when the head grade of the byproduct in the ore is low and exhibits large variations. The test samples should also have a similar mining dilution as the future plant feed. The amount of waste rock in the sample should be based on the ratio of mining dilution during future operation. If no mining plan

has been designed, mining dilution can be assumed at 5–10% for an open pit mine in its early phases, and 10–25% for underground mines. 

The 7hysic-mechanical properties and chemical properties of the test samples should be in agreement with the properties of the ore reserve and the plant feed during the initial stage of operation. Specifically, the following process related features must be determined: 

- Ore density and ore bulk density. 

- Ore moisture. 

- Clay content. 

- Ore oxidization level. 

- Soluble salt content. 

- Ore hardness and other mechanical properties. 

For porphyry copper deposits, typically 200–300 kg of ore sample will be required for the bench scale flotation testing. For a mini-pilot test 500–1,000 kg of sample can be required. Pilot tests typically require several times the quantity of material compared with bench scale tests. The detailed sample weight should be based on the objective and content of the test, the capacity of the test equipment and the duration of test. 

For samples used for the comminution tests, larger pieces of rock sample are preferred—especially for the crushing and SAG test. Typically, at least drill core size of NQ (corresponds to inside core diameter of 47.6 mm) or HQ (corresponds to inside core diameter of 63.5 mm) should be used. For SAG sizing, a large drill core of PQ (75mm) may be required. A large number of sampling locations and sufficient sample weight are imperative to the establishment of a reliable geometallurgical database. This is used not only for plant design but also for plant optimization and improved process control especially in the case of a complex orebody. 

Examples of insufficient sampling, which influenced the quality of testwork and equipment sizing, are discussed in the next section of this paper. **RECENT EXAMPLES—PERSPECTIVES ON TESTWORK AND PLANT DESIGN** 

There are several recent project examples which experienced difficulty in achieving the designed operation performance in terms of mill throughput or concentrate product quality. The sources of the problems from all these examples are from nonoptimized plant designs resulting from a combination of insufficient testwork, lack of testwork planning, lack of ore mineralogy and sampling errors. 

## **Project A – Sub-Saharan Copper Concentrator** 

The orebody is a high-grade copper deposit with head grade around 3% Cu. With this high copper grade in the ore, the client expected high recovery and high-grade concentrates due to the inherent ore mineralogy. However, there was insufficient mineralogical and metallurgical testwork done before the plant was built. The design basis was taken largely from other copper concentrators with different sets of process characteristics. 

After the plant started up, the copper recovery fluctuated around 85% and below the process guarantee. After several plant surveys and additional diagnostic metallurgical and mineralogical studies, it was found that the low recovery was mainly due to the presence of oxide copper in the ore. The flotation circuit was designed to recover sulfide copper minerals, but it was found there was a considerable amount of oxide copper in the ore. Besides chalcocite and chalcopyrite, there were also bornite, covellite and considerable amount of malachite and chrysocolla in the plant feed. The percent of oxide copper against total copper in the ore varied from 10–27%, and without special treatment most oxide copper was lost to the tailings. After testwork, a sulfidizing tank was added to treat the sulfide copper rougher tailings. This increased the copper recovery by an average of 4%. 

Also, the lack of consideration in carrying capacities with high grade concentrates resulted in the undersizing of the cleaner circuit. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

52 

Without testwork, the previous cleaning circuit was based on an assumption to the mass pull of flotation roughers. However, it was found that the rougher mass pull in the plant was much higher than the assumption. In addition, all the concentrate transfer systems, including the pumps, pipelines and launders, were all undersized. After modifying

the circuit with much larger cleaner cells and slurry transport system, the plant recovery reached close to 90%. 

## **Project B - North American Gold Concentrator** 

The plant was designed to process 50,000 mtpd of ROM ore with a conventional SAG Mill-Ball Mill-Pebble Crushing (SABC) circuit. In the project development phase only a small number of samples were selected and tested for the grinding circuit design. This was due to sample availability. In the commercial operation and subsequent ore mapping studies, the ore testing revealed significantly harder ore parameters and the JK drop weight test confirmed the JK a*b value around 20–24, rather than 30–35 as previously measured from the small number of samples tested. The distinct shift of a*b values as described above means a net increase in the SAG specific power of 2–3 kWh/t. So, with the installed mill sizes the plant could only attain 70–75% of the design throughput. As a consequence a pre-crushing circuit before the SAG mill had to be built to achieve the designed plant throughput. This circuit addition cost approximately 5–10% of the overall capital cost, which is significant. Also, running at reduced capacity was very costly to the mine owner. 

## **Project C - CIS Gold Plant** 

The plant includes comminution, flotation, gravity circuit with intense cyanidation, CIL circuit and ADR circuit. Though there had been a lot of testwork performed on the project over a vast period of time, there are several factors that influenced the quality of testwork. They are listed below. 

- Insufficient sampling—the sample used for the testwork had a very different head grade compared to the current head grade of the plant feed 

- Lack of understanding of the relationship of the ore tested and the mine plan requirements 

- There are several process modifications adopted into the design which were not confirmed by the testwork 

- The flotation testwork used an archaic flowsheet configuration, which is very different from the more modern flowsheet used later in the plant 

Due to the above issues, the plant did not achieve its designed plant performance more than one year after plant startup. The actual gold recovery in the plant is almost 20% lower than the designed value, which caused a huge economic loss.

This plant is a large copper molybdenum concentrator, with the plant throughput approximately 115,000 to 120,000 mtpd. At the very early stage of the project, extensive sampling and testwork had been conducted. During the parameters optimization, the testwork was conducted on all three major composite samples. In addition, the ore variabil

ity tests, including the crushing, grinding and flotation, were repeated on 100 individual samples. After laboratory scale testwork, a pilot plant test including two test campaigns was conducted. Each campaign was conducted continuously for five days, on a 24 hours per day basis. During the pilot test trials, problems associated with low molybdenum recovery in the flotation column were detected and a  corresponding circuit modification had been implemented in the plant later. 

Due to the high quality of testwork upfront, the plant was started up within 6 month, and reached the designed plant throughput and recovery. The recovery achieved in the commercial plant is identical to that achieved in the pilot plant, both reaching around 90%.  Since the plant startup, no unexpected process issues influenced the operation. Due to the extensive sampling program, the plant is sufficiently robust to treat different ore types and meet designed plant performance. 

The following sections will introduce the testwork program and planning required for successfully designing and building a typical copper concentrator. 

## **THE SCALE OF TESTWORK** 

Testwork programs are typically initiated via bench scale testing. Bench scale testing is the first choice due to its simplicity, cost and sample size requirements. Depending on the complexity of the orebody and other project-specific requirements, larger scale integrated or pilot plant campaigns may be required. Generally, the scale of the testwork can be classified as follows. 

## **Bench Scale Testwork** 

During the exploration stage, the test plan should be focused on the study of the characteristics of different ore types and ore grade, the basic processing flowsheet concept and possible attainable parameters of the products and tailings, including the achievable product specifications—% metal in concentrate—and the recovery of some economic byproducts. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

54 

This test plan is able to provide sufficient guidance for producing a conceptual PFD (Process Flow Diagram), basic product specifications, the main equipment selection and sizing and some trade-off studies. As it is of small scale, the bench scale testing is frequently used for a proof-of-concept study. As fewer samples and lower cost are required for the test, it allows the exploration of different processing options within a broader scope. It is important to note that bench scale tests on sufficient samples can also give an indication of operating envelopes. 

## **Continuous Lab Test (Mini-Pilot Test)** 

Based on the selected flowsheet determined from the bench scale test, this test is conducted continuously with lab test units to simulate the grinding, separation and dewatering circuits in the industrial operation. More complex hydrometallurgical flowsheets, involving recycle streams etc, can also be tested in this manner. It can also confirm the steady state of the operation if operated over several d

ays, and determine the expected process performance and process parameters. For concentrator process design it will include a small-scale mill and a mini-rig for flotation, including roughing and cleaning stages. The typical test capacity is between 5–20 kg/hr. The mini-pilot plant set up can also be used to test larger quantities of specific ore types. 

These tests should have duration of 24–96 hours. When the flowsheet is complex, or has numerous recycle streams or has adopted a new technology, the test duration should be longer. 

## **Pilot Test** 

When the ore characteristics are complex and little reference exists from the industry, or some new technologies are used in the design or the plant throughput is very large and the process flowsheet and operating parameters from the lab are not sufficient to conclude that the future operation will be stable and reliable, the pilot test should be considered. Financial institutes may also demand that the ore is tested at a full pilot scale level of operation and there may be a need to generate larger quantities of concentrates for subsequent downstream processing. For example, concentrates may be produced for specifications to the smelting companies or a specific downstream process such as concentrate leaching. 

Pilot testing can be conducted on either the whole flowsheet or part of the flowsheet. The objective is to confirm the flowsheet developed from the lab and to acquire the technical and economical performance parameters as close as possible to the plant operation. Besides confirming the flowsheet, some parameters can be further adjusted and optimized in the pilot test. The typical plant throughput is between 0.5–5.0 tons/hour. In the past decade pilot scale grinding test campaigns have followed a standard approach involving evaluation of ore types and circuit energy efficiency, impact of ball loading on SAG mill operation, impact of mill grate opening configuration and pebble ports, open or closed circuit configuration and impact of pebble crushing. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

55 

When there is an economic concentration of molybdenum byproduct in the copper deposit, and the plant throughput is large, a pilot plant run is recommended to generate sufficient bulk concentrate sample for a locked cycle molybdenum flotation testing. 

The duration of a pilot test should be between 72 hours and two weeks, depending on the complexity of the flowsheet. 

## **Full-Scale Industry Testing** 

Industrial testing is conducted in an existing plant, utilizing one line or even the whole plant for the test. It can be either on the whole flowsheet or part of the flowsheet. The technical and economic performance from this testing will be the most reliable for project evaluation. These types of tests may occur when there are vastly different ore types being treated or if the circuit becomes re-configured (e.g. addition of an HPGR into the crushing circuit to debottleneck circuit capacity

constraints). For a typical flowsheet and single circuit, the test duration should be between 5–7 days. For a complex flowsheet the test duration is typically between 10–15 days. If the industry test is on the whole flowsheet to test the production and operation, the duration can be up to six months. ## **Environmental Testing and Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Support** When there are potentially hazardous constituents in the ore, or toxic reagents, and if the local environmental agency has specific requirements, environmental testing may also need to be conducted. Generally, the items below should be considered. - For the process water from the concentrate and tailings streams, any other contaminated water, gaseous emission, tailings material, any bleed stream, if they exceed the limit, a test for waste treatment should be considered. - For any radioactive, asbestiform minerals or any toxic reagents, corresponding safety measures need to be considered. - If possible, to minimize a source of environmental contamination, reagents should avoid using the agents that will damage humans, agriculture, forestry, ranching and fishery. Based on the process design needs, the process engineer should work with other disciplines and list the requirements for the testwork, with the focus on the main process issues and any special technical questions that need to be answered. Below is an example of the main requirements for such a program. ## **Ore C

haracterization** 

The main objective is to determine the mineralogical composition of the ore, including the gangue mineralogy, together with an understanding of the main product mineralogy, liberation and presence of impurities or minerals that can influence the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

57 

process design. Ideally, this step should provide a general guidance for later metallurgical testing. The typical analysis in this step includes: 

- XRD analysis 

- Optical microscopy performance as early as possible 

- Qemscan/MLA or TIMA analysis 

- NIR-CEC analysis 

The importance of sufficient mineralogy testing is often underestimated. However, the benefit of conducting sufficient mineralogy testwork upfront during the project can bring huge profit from better process design and improved plant performance, as illustrated in the figure 2 below. 













Figure 2 – Impact of Early Process Mineralogy to Project Economics (Courtesy of Dr. Norm Lotter, Xstrata Process Support, 2010) 

Some physical characteristics of the ore, including ore density, bulk density, repose angle, internal friction angle and ROM ore moisture, if convenient, should also be measured for future engineering design. These types of tests are normally associated with the crushing testwork and material flow testing. 

## **Comminution Testing** 

The comminution test plan will depend on the expected size reduction option that will be used. In broad terms, comminution circuits follow several main routes: 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

58 

- Stage crushing and ball milling 

- Stage crushing including tertiary HPGR crushing and ball milling 

- Primary crushing and SAG-Ball Milling-Pebble Crushing (SABC) 

In the case of the treatment of oxide copper ores, either a stage crushing followed by heap leach or a stage crushing followed by agitated leaching is used. 

The typical tests required for stage crushing circuit design include Bond crushing working index test and Unconfined Compression Strength (UCS) test. An abrasion test will also be required to estimate the “wear prediction,” the maintenance requirement and spare parts for the crusher. 

For ball mill sizing, the Bond ball mill index test is still universally used. Though the normal closing size for Bond work index is 100 mesh, the closing size is actually a function of product grind size. With the current trend of ore with finer liberation, the closing size should be as close as possible to the grinding product size in the plant, typically one sieve size coarser than the cyclone overflow P80. To simulate the continuous steady state operation in the plant, the Bond work index test should be conducted with at least six cycles. Sufficient tests should be conducted based on different sample lots to get a distribution of Bond work indices. In order to maintain the designed mill throughput in spite of ore hardness variation, typically 75 percentile of Bond work index—or the average va

lue plus one standard deviation—is used for mill sizing. 

The accuracy of the Bond ball mill work index test can influence the ball mill product P80 size. Flotation feed P80 size always has a close relationship with the flotation recovery, and Figure 3 shows the relationship between mill product P80 and flotation recovery for one project. For this ore, every 1 micron coarser corresponds to 0.1% flotation recovery loss. The impact to the project economy is quite significant for large concentrators. 

For SAG mill sizing, there are different methodologies based on different philosophies. Currently, the most widely used SAG tests are the JK drop weight test and the Starkey SAG design test, together with Bond crushing work index, rod mill work index and Bond ball mill work index. The JK drop weight test and SAG design test are widely used for SAG mill sizing. Figure 4 shows the illustration of the JK drop weight test and a picture of the SAG design test unit. Some other tests on SAG sizing include the SMC test and Minnovex SPI test, though these tests are partially related to the previous two test methodologies. To get more reliable test results for SAG sizing, it is recommended that all three sets of tests to be conducted. If full JK drop weight tests are not conducted then the SMC test approach should be considered. Again, a sufficient number of tests should be conducted in order to get a distribution of ore hardness data. In larger projects the trend for mining companies is to have the grinding circuit sized and validated by 2–4 independent grinding experts, together with consultation from the mill supplier and its associated experts. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

59

Figure 4 – JK drop weight test illustration (left) & SAG design test unit picture (right) 

When there is a significant amount of clay material in the sample, the clay or slime content should be measured, as clay has considerable impact on grinding performance. This can result in a less conventional circuit design involving more than one stage of classification. 

For regrind applications, nowadays the tower mill, Vertimill and Isamill are more popular than conventional ball mills due to their energy efficiency. These types of mills typically use small sized media (typically ceramic) which provides a large surface for grinding and offe ~~rs~~ a range of media densities. These types of tests should be conducted 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

60 

by the manufacturer with a representative sample. During the last three years the VSX mill technology has gained interest with a growing number of installations and is an economical alternative to the Vertimill and Isamill. 

High Pressure Grinding Roll (HPGR) technology is gaining more importance. In the past few years the number of HPGR circuits has increased, particularly in the base and precious

metal sectors. With increasingly harder ores and higher power costs in certain regions of the world, the HPGR approach is more than worthy of consideration. There has been a greater acceptance in the heap leach applications as well. Baum (2011) had revealed many benefits by using HPGR in the copper heap leach operation. The key for quality HPGR testwork is an appropriately sized test unit, since the small test unit can skew the test result and is difficult to treat a representative sample feed. In addition, the HPGR testing should be performed by a lab with extensive HPGR experience. 

## **Mineral Processing** 

For most porphyry copper operations around the world, flotation is still the predominant processing method to concentrate copper sulphide minerals. 

For the flotation testing, the parameters to be investigated include: 

- The optimum grind size for maximizing flotation recovery 

- The slurry density 

- Slurry pH (sometimes temperature is also a parameter to consider) 

- Reagent schedule 

- Flotation residence time and kinetic determination 

- Impact of process water chemistry 

For copper flotation, especially for a byproduct moly circuit, there can be numerous stages of cleaning. One of the objectives for the flotation test is to find the optimum flotation flowsheet. Besides determining the number of cleaner stages, the arrangement of cleaner scavengers also needs to be considered. It’s important to investigate the characteristics of middling streams, whether these should be recycled or whether there is a need for independent treatment. The investigation of middling and tailings streams during flotation can also help to understand some issues related to low recovery and low concentrate grade, which helps to adjust the flowsheet and test plan accordingly. 

To simulate the recycle stream, locked cycle testing is the most effective method except for a continuous pilot test. To be representative of the commercial operation, the locked cycle test has to reach equilibrium through numerous cycles. Figure 5 illustrates the locked cycle test reaching the equilibrium, as well as not reaching equilibrium. The number of cycles required to converge depends on the number of cleaner stages and complexity of the flowsheet. Sometimes, due to the scarcity of ore samples, a composite sample is acceptable for the test. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

61 











Figure 5 – Locked cycle test equilibrium 

For orebodies with large ore variation, a flotation variability testing should be considered. This will give a better indication of the variation of flotation performance, which can be used for better process design. It will also provide the basis for geometallurgical modeling. These tests are usually performed after flotation parameters have been established. 

Complex ore mineralogy, soluble salts or a complex reagent scheme will eventually impact the water chemistry, which can have a significant influence on flotation. In thi

s case, the process water should be saved for further flotation testing, expanded continuous lab tests or pilot tests. 

Typically, a laboratory unit flotation cell can predict the performance of a commercial mechanical cell, but it cannot be used to predict the performance of a flotation column. To simulate the performance of a flotation column, at least one pilot unit should be used to provide any meaningful data. Considering the solids/bubble distribution homogeneity across the section, there should be a safety factor in sizing the column. 

Copper oxides are generally difficult to float, though they can be sulfidized and subsequently floated. Nevertheless, some copper oxides, such as chrysocolla, cannot be floated after sulfidization. If the content of this type of copper oxide is high in the ore or the economics favor acid leach, tank leach or heap leach can be considered. In the leach test, some general parameters should be monitored, including pH level, optimum particle size, retention time and acid dosage. If a column leach test is the basis for a leach test, special attention should be paid to the column size, ore mineralogy (whether acid consuming gangue minerals exists), crush size, agglomeration, acid addition rate, bed porosity, test duration, solution strength and liquor analysis. If there is precious metal in 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

62 

the ore as a byproduct, cyanide leach testing should also be conducted to evaluate the economics. 

## **Dewatering Tests** 

Sedimentation (thickening) and filtration tests are also required for process design. For a typical copper concentrator, the required tests for design include the tailing sedimentation test, concentrate sedimentation test and concentrate filtration test. 

For all dewatering tests, the feed stream should be characterized, including PSD (particle size distribution), solid specific gravity, liquid specific gravity, soluble salt (if any), pH and feed solids concentration. Ideally the data on mineralogy composition should also be recorded. The sedimentation test should then provide following parameters; 

- Optimum diluted feed solids concentration by weight 

- Expected underflow density and overflow clarity as a function of residence time 

- Flocculent type and recommended dosage 

- Thickener size (both diameter and underflow retention time) 

- Underflow solids yield stress as a function of solids concentration by weight 

It is recommended to run both static settling tests and continuous fill tests. Although sedimentation pilot testing occurs less frequently, it can provide additional information for process design, especially for some newer types of equipment such as paste and high density thickeners, or for an ore feed that has large variation and difficult to get a representative sample, or if the water chemistry in the whole process circuit is complex. 

Rheology data on the settled solids is used for the raking mechanism design and drive torqu

e specification. Underflow rheology also provides critical information for pump and piping design especially when the tailings thickener underflow has to be pumped to a distant tailings dam. 

One issue of sedimentation test is sample aging, which can influence the accuracy of the test results. The water chemistry will also influence the sedimentation performance and flocculent screening. If the ore has a large variation and different ore will be mined at different time period, the ore sample from different ore types should be tested separately to determine the variation in sedimentation characteristics. 

Filtration is typically conducted on the concentrate, however with current trends of stricter environmental regulation and scarcity of water source, tailing filtration is beginning to emerge in the industry. Based on the mechanism of filtration, the filtration tests can be either vacuum filtration or pressure filtration. The sample should be representative, or variability tests should be considered if the ore variation is large, as the variation in ore type or mineralogy in a mine can significantly affect filterability of flotation concentrate. The solids concentration of filtration feed should be same with the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

63 

upstream thickener underflow. The slurry pH, ORP and reagent dosage should also be as close as possible to the future operation. 

Similar to sedimentation, sample aging may also considerably influence filtration performance. For example, certain sulfide concentrates from flotation which is relatively reactive, can change with time and alter the filtration characteristics. The sample for filtration test should be as fresh as possible. In addition, sample should not be dried, or frozen, or dewatered and then repulped for the filtration test, as the sample may behave differently after these procedures. The temperature should also be recorded as it will influence the slurry viscosity and consequently the filtration rate. 

## **Reporting** 

After completing all the testwork, a quality test report must be provided to the client and process design team for the project advancement. The test report should have sufficient defined information and reliable data, and a thorough analysis which can be used to set out the process parameters and basic process equipment design. The content of the report should include: 

- The objective and requirement of the testwork 

- An evaluation of sample representativeness and sample selection information 

- The summary of ore characterization tests 

- Mineral processing test descriptions, including crushing, grinding, flotation, acid leaching (for oxide copper), cyanide leaching (for gold as byproduct), sedimentation and filtration 

- Test plans and selection of test equipment should be determined; the optimum test condition will be explored and a figure of the test flowsheet test will be proposed based on the exploration test 

- The variability test ne

eds to be completed 

- Back up appendices of all the respective test conditions, etc. 

- Tailing characteristics for tailings deposition and geo-technical considerations 

- Environmental protection test, if necessary 

- Technical and economical evaluation 

- further recommendations 

- Any appendices, tables, figures, references and data

## **CONCLUSIONS** 

The mining industry continues to face challenges with resource quality, mineralogical complexity and more complex processing routes. The net impact is that project capital and operating costs have increased and profit margins on new projects are at different levels than they used to be. At the same time the technical skill set resource shortage has also increased the risks on project development. With larger plants and larger equipment in the market, the risk associated with quality of testwork and equipment sizing is even higher. Any mistake from the testwork and design can lead to a huge economic risk and loss, sometimes resulting in projects failing to meet their expectations in terms of capacity or product quality. 

Testwork costs as a percentage of the overall project cost are often less than 2% and yet it does not receive the focus or scope definition it deserves. 

Mining projects often have aggressive schedules that result in several activities proceeding in parallel. Testwork planning and correctness cannot be underestimated. As illustrated in Figure 6, the bench scale flotation testwork contributes to the success of a huge investment. Minimizing the technical risk is of prime importance to new projects, and avoiding the common mistake on testwork programs and planning—too little, too late—must be fully recognized.
