## **Results of the operations and projects geometallurgical survey** 

The main conclusions and recommendations derived from the survey conducted by JK-Tech, taking into account that the same was conducted with the information provided by each site (information frozen as of Dec. 2012) plus a field visit are: 

Generating a data base integrated to the mining, metallurgical, geological, and mineralogical data. 

Using an iterative Geometallurgical Unit determination process (UGM) by considering the representativeness, variability, significance, or impact on the business, focusing the effort in those aspects that will be more significant in defining the design 

73 

criteria, production goals (geo - mining  - metallurgical criteria), as well in identifying and quantifying the business risks. 

UGM definitions should be continuously modified against the block model parameters. This process requires detailed mineralogical and geochemical analyses. 

The geometallurgical sampling includes variability in the mineralogical, geochemical samples, and metallurgical tests. To identify variability, it should be carefully controlled and focused. This includes selecting the sample to define a parameter's potential ranges, as well as the quantity control, distribution, and type of sample material. Sample correlation should be carried out with the same type of drillings, tests, and similar intervals, as well as spatial and statistics. 

A core element in the geometallurgical programs is the creation and building of the specialist teams.  To this respect, no homogeneity is observed in the personal composition and quality assigned to geometallurgy, both in projects and operations. Management is recommended to define the minimum teams, the adequate profiles, and a team building plan. 

## **Corporate Geometallurgical Guidelines** 

The development type or level of the geometallurgical model should depend on the project stage, for which a higher detail in the ADS related to this matter is not required.  To develop this matter, work teams will be built. 

The number of samples should be based on each ore field's reality and the company's vision regarding risk aversion (the more aversion, the more samples are required to lower uncertainty). 

A QA/QC plan or analysis should always be considered in any development model or development stage, both for chemical and mineralogical analysis, and for metallurgical tests. 

Any resource or planning estimation model should investigate and quantify the error associated  to the estimation. 

It is relevant generating geological models which, from their early stage in the projects, report the geological variables that can have an impact on the process, both advantageous and deleterious.  Recognizing the mineralogical distinct mark and the geochemistry of each ore field, its space distribution, textures, etc., will help to establish domains likely to turn into a common language with the metallurgists. 

74

The geometallurgical variables to be modeled will firstly depend on the process (flotation, leaching), the most common ones being the metallurgical recovery, concentrate grade, plant treatment, mineralogy, deleterious effects typical to each ore field, acid consumption. 

## **CONCLUSIONS** 

This project is in progress, and counting on defined corporate guidelines to develop the Geometallugy both of operations and projects at the end of 2013 is intended. Following this study, it can be seen that standardizing, in spite of the differences typical to the ore fields, is feasible. 

A top up and down spreading will be made within AMSA organization, which will allow to create value as well as a culture or group quality sign through a learning process, since the whole organization shall align and work on a jointly basis, thus creating not only a change in metallurgy but a most holistic way of facing processes.

## **ABSTRACT** 

Compaснa Minera Doсa Inйs de Collahuasi SCM initiated the development of its geometallurgical modelling in 2007. The original objective was to characterize the Rosario deposit in terms of the yearly treatment capacity. The grinding model allows predicting the treatment capacity, specific power and balls consumption for short, mid and long term planning. 

Also, the model allows detecting the constraints of the grinding circuits and prioritizes these restrictions to define projects to release them. This is important for the Capex estimation during the budget planning every year. 

The model uses a combination of simulation and power-based approaches to relate ore hardness and flotation feed size to grinding circuit throughput. Ore hardness values are provided by Collahuasi’s block model which has been populated with ore characterisation data derived from Bond ball work index tests, JK drop-weight tests and SMC Tests<sup>®</sup> on diamond drill cores 

Additionally, an alternative impact test to estimate SAG grinding parameters is also presented to bring the geometallurgical model from mid and long term to short term planning. The impact test uses either the production bench or geological drill holes. This allows Geologists increasing the density of grinding parameters within the block model improving the geostatistical estimation of the rest of the blocks. 

The grinding model has been successfully used in mining planning and the accuracy of the model is demonstrated

using monthly average instantaneous throughput from January to August 2013, showing an average relative error of 6% and an _R_<sup>_2_</sup> value of 0.9.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

During the last years many mining companies have invested significantly geometallurgy  as they have increasingly realised that constructive integration of geology, mining and processing aspects into a so-called “Geometallurgical model” pays financial dividends through being able to maximize the throughput and efficiency of their treatment plants in both short and long-term time frames (Alruiz, 2009; Suazo, 2010). 

In practice, from a comminution perspective, an effective Geometallurgical model should be able to forecast accurately the throughput of the grinding circuit from information provided by the mine plan on the nature and quantity of ores that are to be delivered to the processing plant. To do so, there are at least six important requirements for the model.  These are as follows: 

Sufficient and relevant samples have been identified, extracted and tested to ensure the required definition and resolution on a block-by-block basis in the mine plan; 

Appropriate breakage tests have been chosen to describe comminution properties of the different rock types (units) in the ore body; 

The model(s) chosen to describe the comminution equipment in the circuit respond realistically to changes in breakage properties as described by the chosen breakage tests; 

All of the above are integrated into an overall description of the on-line operational response of the grinding circuit that takes into account non-ore related influences and which can be easily integrated into the existing block model. 

- The daily constrains in grinding circuit must be recorded. These are related to the peripheral equipment (conveyors, pumps, etc.) that constraints throughput when they are not available due to unprogrammed shut downs. 

- The final model can convincingly demonstrate its accuracy through validation using real operational data. 

Each of these aspects has been comprehensively tackled at Compaснa Minera Doсa Inйs de Collahuasi SCM (Collahuasi) in its development of a Geometallurgical model for its “Rosario” deposit and these will be described in the following sections.

Figure 6. Variability samples and DWi values ## **DESCRIPTION OF THE COLLAHUASI GRINDING CIRCUIT** The Concentrator operating facilities start with the primary crusher at the Rosario pit. Crushed ore is transported by overland conveyor to the 100,000 metric tonnes coarse ore stockpile in front of the three SABC grinding circuits. The initial circuit included two grinding lines and achieved full production in October 1998. A third grinding line was installed during a subsequent expansion, with full production being achieved in April 2004. The first two identical grinding lines (Lines 1 and 2) consist of one 32 x 13.5ft (8,000 kW installed power) SAG, in series with one 22 x 36ft (8,000 kW) ball mill. The third grinding line (Line 3) consists of one 40 x 22ft (21,000 kW) SAG mill working with two 26 x 38ft (15,500 kW each) ball mills. The SAG mill trommel oversize product (pebbles) is sent to the pebble crushing plant, consisting of two pebble crushers in parallel. Crushed pebbles are returned to the coarse ore stockpile. The ball mills work in a reverse classification circuit, in which the hydrocyclone underflow feeds into the ball mills and the hydrocyclone overflow is sent to the flotation circuit. The current daily average throughput of Collahuasi´s grinding circuit is 150,000 metric tonnes per day with an average product size ( _P80_ ) of approximately 210 microns. 7 82 ## **CONMINUTION CIRCUIT MODELLING** Originally, every single variability sample was simulated individually using JKSimmet. ## **INTRODUCTION** 

Compaснa Minera Doсa Inйs de Collahuasi SCM initiated the development of a new geometallurgical model to characterize its Rosario deposit in terms of its comminution circuit capacity (Alruiz et al., 2009) and flotation performance (Suazo et al., 2010, 2012). 

It is well known that the flotation process is affected, among other factors, by the dispersion of bubbles and particles. The dispersion of gas into bubbles – gas dispersion – has a key impact on the flotation performance, as described in the literature (Schwartz and Alexander, 2006). Gas dispersion in the collection zone can be characterized by several variables, namely, the superficial gas velocity ( _Jg_ ), the gas holdup ( ε _g_ ), the Sauter mean bubble size ( _db_ ), and the bubble surface area flux ( _Sb=6Jg/db_ ). The latter being perhaps the most important gas dispersion property since it represents the flux of available bubble surface for flotation. 

Scaling-up laboratory results to industrial scale is a fundamental problem both for designing new operations and for the optimization of existing ones. 

In the current approach, the flotation rate constant for different Collahuasi’s ore types of Collahuasi (geometallurgical unit, UGM, from the Spanish “Unidad <u>GeoMetalurgica”) are modelled as a function of the gas dispersion properties and the</u> flotation feed particle size distribution, along with operational and equipment parameters. The approach has the advantage of allowing the simulation of flotation performance at different scales. The model introduces a parameter ( Φ ), characteristic of the ore type, that can be used to scale-up results from the laboratory to industrial scale. 

The flotation rate constant was scaled up from laboratory scale to pilot scale and also to industrial scale. A flotation piloting test was performed in order to compare the estimated flotation rate constant (using the approach presented in this article) and the experimental rate obtained from a kinetic survey performed on the pilot plant. Similar work was performed on the industrial flotation circuit of Collahuasi Mining Company.

The model considers the probability of flotation and includes a parameter Φ that accounts for the inherent floatability of the mineral. The parameter Φ is a key component in the model, it is characteristic of the ore type or geometallurgical unit and it does not depe

nd on the scale of the flotation process. Once Φ is determined, it is possible to scale-up the kinetics parameter in order to estimate copper recoveries at industrial scale. This approach was tested with data collected from the production records at Collahuasi’s concentrator (from January to August 2013). The results showed a good prediction of the actual recovery, with an average relative error of 1.8%.

## **ABSTRACT** 

This paper summarizes the activities performed to predict SAG milling throughput at Minera Esperanza. 

Having highly reliable geometallurgical models aided by the new computer tools and specific metallurgical testing to rely on has become a major issue in recent times due to their impact on the business. 

Minera Esperanza’s SAG throughput model was constructed by characterizing the ore feed and operational parameters of the plant. Producing a robust model required satisfying number of requirements for the parameters used for both the ore and the plant as follow: 1) geologic and geometallurgical characterization parameters; and 2) parameters of a plant running at the rated production under optimum operating conditions. Obtaining these parameters required increasing the quantity of samples and metallurgical testing through drilling campaigns, mapping the drill holes and putting samples through various comminution tests while sampling all operational flows at the plant to obtain the metallurgical information for the operational parameters. 

The information was entered on the JKSimMet software to enable a throughput model to be developed to output SAG mill throughput predictions that are very close to actual throughput figures, i.e., accurate within a range of 2% on a monthly basis.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

This paper summarizes the activities carried out by the Minera Esperanza geometallurgy team to predict SAG milling throughput by implementing a work methodology to estimate throughput capacity at Esperanza’s concentrator plant on the basis of ore feed and operating conditions with the aid of metallurgical software (JKSimMet). 

To enable Esperanza’s throughput model output data to adequately match actual throughput, the model must satisfy a number of requirements regarding the parameters to represent the ore feed and the plant, viz.: having a geologic and geometallurgical characterization to rely on and having the plant running at its rated capacity under optimal operating conditions when performing the sampling for model calibration. 

To provide these parameters, drilling campaigns were performed with the drill holes mapped and samples obtained for various comminution tests. Meanwhile, samples were taken at the plant t

o determine the operating parameters. 

The combined data obtained were processed on the JKSimMet software to enable the development of a SAG milling throughput model with optimum results that allow plant throughput predictions to be made with an accuracy of 2% on a monthly basis. 

The Esperanza concentrator plant processes low-grade copper sulfide ore with gold contents. The principal ore minerals are chalcopyrite, bornite and scarce chalcocite and covellite. The principal lithology consists of andesite, porphyries and dacite. The processing of the sulfide ore is by means of SAG milling with the SAG mill operating in an SABC-B circuit, and the downstream flotation concentration process operates with a blend of sea water (30%), pumped in from an intake in the Michilla area on the Pacific coast, and process water (70%). The throughput design capacity of the plant is 97,000 tpd to produce approximately 685 kt/year of concentrate grading an average 28% copper with an overall copper recovery of 90%. 

## **PERFORMANCE OF THE WORK** 

## **The Challenge** 

The Minera Esperanza geometallurgical area set as an objective the creation of adequate geometallurgical models for the deposit that with the capability of outputting results that have the least variability possible to better aid in reducing the uncertainty involved in mine plans. 

In the pursuit of this objective, a two-stage work program was prepared. The first stage focused on evaluating the existing SAG throughput model, with it found that this model was overestimating the values expected. The second stage was designed in view of this finding to generate a new cutting edge SAG milling throughput prediction model,

i.e., a model featuring new concepts of both metallurgical test work and the use of process simulators that are reproducible based on geologic and operating information. 

Accordingly, the model required had to be based on variables that can be updated and/or modified independently and that is flexible enough for purposes of evolving along with the optimizations made in the plant over a short- or long-term horizon. 

## **Working Methodology** 

The work defined was organized essentially into the following stages of development: 

- Obtaining information.

Figure 1- Modeling process work flow. ## **Definition of the Scope of the Model** In general, throughput capacity has been analyzed by considering the plant only. On the side of the plant, the current configuration of the grinding circuit includes a SAG mill, two ball mills and three pebble crushers, and the comminution process output is restricted by the throughput capacity of the SAG mill (viz., by the mill installed power and mill fill level). In this connection, this study considered that the process of reduction in size does not depend on the conventional plant equipment (SAG mill, ball mills, etc) only, but rather can be viewed as a complete sequence that starts with the blasting process. Accordingly, the result of SAG milling was defined as also depending on upstream processes, such as blasting and crushing. A tool that makes it possible to include all of these variables in one single model is the metallurgical process simulation software. For this study, a decision was made to work with the JKSimMet software, which makes it possible to integrate coherently and efficiently all of these restrictions, enabling a virtual replica of the plant in a stationary state to be generated (called simulation), thus allowing corresponding operational results to be visualized when modifying variables of interest. Accordingly, a simulation was generated covering from the blasting process on downstream to the SAG milling product. Using this simulation and statistical tools, an _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 117 equation was obtained to predict the result of the expected throughput under certain operating conditions. ## **Configuration and Calibration** Configuration and calibration consist of creating the design of the plant to be simulated on the JKSimMet software; this involves replicating all of the production circuit. This stage is crucial because the software makes it possible to interact with each element created as if it were an actual piece of equipment. The configuration of all of the plant equipment was performed with the support of the company Split Engineering. Thereafter, and to achieve correct calibration, the simulator must be calibrated using real operational data. This calibration is performed by means of sampling at specific positions of the plant. For example, to obtain the particle size distribution of the ore input to the SAG milling process, samplin

g is performed on the SAG mill feed belt. In addition, the operating parameters of all equipment entered into the simulator are used, e.g., power, velocities, trommel opening, crusher settings, mill fill level, etc. 

## **<u>Simulation</u>** 

In simulation, the stage following calibration, it is possible to simulate the results of the complete process from crusher feed on downstream to the feeding of ore to rougher flotation by varying the operating conditions and the characteristics of the ore. This underscores why the calibration process is a key part of this model. 

With the model calibrated it is possible to obtain equations as a function of operating parameters and the characteristics of the ore, such as specific energy consumption (SEC) and Axb (Figure 2).

An adequate calibration combined the results of the metallurgical campaign make it possible to generate a robust database to enable a predictive model to be generated of the ore to be processed. 

Equation 1 shows the capacity of the SAG milling circuit, which is defined by the quotient between the resources input to milling, measured as the power draft of the drive system and the size reduction work performed. Equation 2 shows the effect of varying the feed ore particle size distribution only while leaving the operating parameters unchanged. 



The power draft is a function of the internal dimensions of the mill, design of the mill liners, speed of rotation, ball mill fill level and charge. 

The work of size reduction performed is a function of an ore hardness indicator (Axb) and the feed-product particle size distribution. The critical sizes (Cs) and percentages in the feed particle size consist are determined, defining for the JK Model 36%, for example, the following Cs percentages: 36% < 1 ¼ in and 16%>4 in.

The leached zone (LX) thickness varies between 40 and 400 m and it is characterized by associations of limonitic minerals, principally jarosite, goethite and hematite. The thickness of the oxide zone (OX) varies between 10 and 200 m and includes associations of copper sulphates and silicates, basically chalcanthite, brocantite, clays with copper and minor chrysocolla and turquoise; chalcanthite is the predominant sulphate in the area, it is associated with rocks with quartz-sericite alteration, and occurs generally in fractures. The thickness of the secondary sulphide zone (SS) reaches in some sectors about 370 m and it is characterized by mineral associations of pyrite-chalcocitechalcopyrite and lesser proportions of coveline. In general, the primary zone (SP) is located in the deepest part of the deposit and corresponds to a hypogene mineralization in which the mineral associations observed are mainly chalcopyrite, pyrite, molybdenite and magnetite.

## **Copper Concentrate Grade Model** 

The copper concentrate grade in the production plan was estimated with geological information with the mining plan and with the metallurgical model prepared with the pilot plant flotation tests results. 

As can be seen in Figure 12, the flotation tests results showed that the main copper concentrate minerals in the project are copper minerals, pyrite and non-sulphide minerals. The copper minerals composition and the proportion of copper minerals –pyrite – non-sulphide minerals determine the copper concentrate grade of the project. The analysis of the result indicates the following: 

- The composition of sulphide copper minerals in the concentrate is similar to that of the feed. 

- The copper sulphide minerals/pyrite weight ratio in the concentrate is a function of that of the feed. 

- The non-sulphide mineral proportion in the concentrate is relatively constant. 

- The result of the flotation feed sequential assay allows approximating the copper mineralogy in the material.

## **PLANT DESIGN** 

Based on the hardness model and metallurgical comminution tests, the plant capacity and its configuration were defined using the following main design criteria: 

- Using one SAG mill and two balls mills, with the biggest sizes in the market. 

- Minimizing the use of water in the project. 

Through the CEET software, simulations defined the average treatment capacity of the plant at 105 KTPD ore, operating with the alternative of recirculating grinding pebbles to the SAG mill (40 feet and 32,000 hp) and two ball mills (27 feet and 27,000 hp). 

Using laboratory and pilot flotation tests, the configuration and size of the equipment for the copper bulk flotation and Mo selective flotation circuits were defined. 

The alternative of optimized water usage was defined by testing the tailings treatment at laboratory and pilot level by: 

- Cycloning the rougher tailings and disposing of the sands in a dump designed to recover their water drainage. 

- Mixing and thickening the scavenger tailings and the cyclone overflow, and then depositing them in a rock fill dam built with borr

## **ABSTRACT** 

Heap leaching is a simple, low-cost method of recovering metals from low grade ores, which has come into widespread application in the mining industry and widely used. To estimate sound metallurgical parameters: recovery of copper and acid consumption, a geometallurgical model is required to be developed. The best way is incorporate a large amount of information with a wide spatial distribution in the resource as it is the chemical analysis of drill and blast hole. The aim of this paper is to present a methodology to develop a geometallurgical model for heap leaching of copper oxides ores. This modeling is based on the geological information and chemical analysis of core drilling and blast hole, laboratory and pilot plant testing, exploratory data analysis for developing the copper extraction and acid consumption geometallurgical models. The end result is a geometallurgical model incorporated in the three-dimensional block model, allowing estimating the copper recovery and acid consumption. The validation of this methodology is carried out with the incorporation of operational information o

f the processing of the ore. This modeling should be used for short, medium and long term planning. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 134 ## **INTRODUCTION** Geometallurgy is a multidisciplinary, applied science that studies both the geology of ore deposits and their metallurgical behaviour. The information is obtained from various sources depending on whether it is a greenfield, brownfield project or a full production plant. However, it is important to maintain the same standard at all of the ore deposit life-cycle. This paper will analyze information from the Radomiro Tomic deposit and illustrate how different sources of information can provide valuable knowledge to the plant process. The basic sources of information used will be exploration drilling, blasting wells and the mineral processed. All three are related to each other through geological mapping, chemical analysis and geometallurgical tests. Interrelating different sources of information is not a simple task. There are basic requirements for this task to be successful and deliver valuable information to the process. Among these requirements are adequate geological mineral characterization, laboratory and pilot plant tests that meet the needs of the mining process and, the use of mathematical tools that allow different responses to be scaled up. The main tools used are spatial averages comparative graphs, pie charts, graphs probabilistic, segmentation tools and classification trees. Which tool to use depends upon the characteristics of the ore and technology used. ## **EXPERIMENTAL** ## **Geological Databases** The first task for a proper geometallurgical analysis is to design a geological database. If there is no suitable geological survey available, geometallurgical samples must be characterized in term of both ore and gangue, because both groups contribute at different stages of the mineral process. ## **Sample Selection for Geometallurgical Tests** 

The main requirement for geometallurgical sample selection is to use the information of the geological model; lithology, alteration and mineralization models. In this way it is possible to carry out the first screening of geometallurgical samples, according to the volume ratio associated with each UGE. In Radomiro Tomic, the geological units are; superior oxide; structural oxide; lower oxide; carbonate oxide; oxide sulphide mixture, weak secondary sulfide, sulfate oxide, strong secondary sulfide and, gravel exotic. Taking samples of the UGE will assure that minerals with similar geological compositions are analyzed together, which in turn will help to define geometallurgical behaviour. 

The variables to be studied in geometallurgical tests are wide-ranging and aim to define envelopes of geological features that control the chemical and physical behavior of minerals, such as copper recovery and acid consumption. However, analysis is also carried out to determine the impurities present in the solutions, the physical quality of the mineral, the dissolution kinetics and copper extraction, among others. All this analyses characterizes the mineral in a new way, differentiating the geometallurgic units (Spanish acronym UGM) from UGE.

## **Definition of a Standard Test of Leaching** 

To define geometallurgical domains reliable measurement and analysis techniques are needed and one challenge is to have a very big number of samples, preferable from thousands to hundreds of thousands. The techniques must be fast, inexpensive and preferentially fully automated. On the other hand, high-quality sampling and testing is quite expensive and is often not possible for sampling constrain. 

In the oxide ore, a standard leaching test has been used at Radomiro Tomic to determine the variability of copper extraction and acid consumption. This test is done for the whole core samples, at the same support as the total copper chemical analysis. Every sample has also the chemical analysis, mineral mapping, spatiality, some physical properties, etc. The standard test is usually carried out for a 10 gram sample with a concentrated sulphuric acid solution that for RT is 1N sulfuric acid, for 30 minutes at 170 rpm. These conditions should be tailored for each particular orebody in terms of acid concentration, mass sample requirements, time of analysis, etc. There are occasions where the mineral also requires others test to determine other properties in the leaching process. In these cases, the standard test can be performed by adding ferric or ferrous ion to the solution. ## **Definition of UGMs** 

Once the analysis of the selected samples has been completed, the UGM are determined. These units must fulfill several conditions to ensure they are the best possible selection. These conditions include: each UGM must represent a significant portion of the ore, different UGMs must have a different means and variance between them depending on the target variable for which they were built. It is common to find separate UGM for copper extraction and acid consumption. It is unusual to find UGMs that explain both characteristics of the process simultaneously. The zones or geometallurical units already determined contribute to the proper selection of metallurgical samples for the process design and production, mining planning and, in particular to a better understanding of the geology and its impact on the mineral leaching process. 

Having built the preliminary geometallurgical model, validation is necessary and a significant amount of samples are needed to accomplish this task. These samples are obtained by a larger diameter drilling, to ensure sufficient mineral for the experimental program. Usually, at this stage larger geometallurgical tests are carried out on unitary columns such as tests in unit columns (one meter high) and also column higher high and diameter and/or one cubic meter container. The purpose of this step is to scale up the results obtained previously and to determine the effect of new variables, such as the ore particle size and the effect of various solutions with impurities, the kinetics of copper extraction and acid consumption. This step may be repeated as often as is necessary, with larger samples, but once completed the result is a geometallurgical model ready for field evaluation. ## **INTRODUCTION** 

Compaснa Minera Doсa Inйs de Collahuasi SCM has developed a grinding parameters Model (GPM) for the Rosario deposit, located in the Cordillera de Domeyko, 120 km southeast of the city of Iquique and 4.800 meters above the sea level. Rosario is a porphyry copper - molybdenum deposit located in the Eocene - Oligocene metallogenic belt that also includes the Ujina, Quebrada Blanca, Chuquicamata and Escondida deposits. 

The GPM model contains the variables required to calculate, through the equations of treatment and specific energy consumption, the values of TPH and CEE for each block, respectively. This model is required for long-term mine planning and for the different business cases. 

The development of this model, and its annual updates begins with the geometallurgical drilling campaign from which the samples are drawn with 10-meter drill core sections, to obtain the mass to carry out grinding tests. 

Quality control made to the Bond test guaranties that the tests, and therefore the values given, are reliable to be used in the estimation process. 

Based on the statistical analysis of the data, it was determined that the lithology is the main control for the grinding parameters. We defined two estimation domains, grouping them by their lithological units. These two domains were called "Porphyry" and "Bedrock" respectively.

## **ABSTRACT** 

The design of a copper concentration plant needs to have a sound geometallurgical and metallurgical test program that includes laboratory and pilot plant tests. Geometallurgical models are important in the design of sulphide concentration plants in greenfield and brownfield projects, as well as in their operation. The purpose of this paper is to explain and provide a methodology to develop a geometallurgical model for copper concentration and have sound design parameters. This modeling is based on the analysis of the geological information commonly acquired for the geological model, metallurgical testing information, and statistical analysis. The modeling stages are: geological information of ore; laboratory and pilot plant tests; exploratory data analysis; geometallurgical model; block model of the deposit with the estimation of parameters; incorporation of values and analysis in the plant design criteria. The end result of this process is a geometallurgical model incorporated in the three-dimensional block model, allowing the estimate of the copper recovery and hardness and, accuracy/precision.  This geometallurgical model and metallurgical test program will be the bases for determining the design parameters.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

In recent years various projects have been carried out. Some of these projects have difficulty reaching the plant design. Factors contributing to technical risk include inadequate information on resources, reserves, development, process metallurgy, product quality and, capacity. A fault in any of the technical fundamentals can have a devastating effect on the outcome and has the potential to destroy a project and ultimately a company. 

Ore reserves and resources are one of the most important and if there is a problem with the basic understanding, the whole project development can become misguided with all conclusions being in effect meaningless. Ore reserves are out of our objectives and will not developed further 

Geometallurgy and Metallurgy are the second most likely technical issues encountered in failure of mining projects (the first being geological/reserve problems). The major issues result from the inadequacy of testing, starting with the selection of representative samples reflecting the variability of the ore, inadequate laboratory, pilot plant testing, scaled-up prototype equipment and modelling, design flaws of the proposed processing method, hardness, etc. Such problems result in low plant recoveries, low throughput, or occasionally contamination of the product. All of which can reduce revenue of the project. 

The aim of conducting Geometallurgical modelling and mapping studies is to reduce the risk of new operations and to improve performance of the plants in operation. Geometallurgical modelling is a multistage process designed to obtain a fundamental

understanding of factors and critical controls that can influence ore processing. Therefore, is essential to understand and carry out the correct test for the design. Geometallurgical modelling is used to scientifically manage risk in project evaluation, for plant design and production forecasting and optimization of production planning and mineral processing unit operations. ## **DEVELOPMENT GEOMETALLURGICAL MODEL** Good feasibility projects are conducted where geologists, mining engineers, and process metallurgists have cooperated in the planning and execution of the sampling and test work early in the development cycle, at the scoping study level (SS), preliminary engineering assessment (PEA), prefeasibility study (PFS), and at the feasibility study stage (FS), to ensure that proper planning for design of the plant is done. Geometallurgy and metallurgy are essential to determine the variability of parameters important in the design of a plant. Figure 2– Generation of geometallurgical model sample selection ## **Sample Selection** The selection of samples that form the foundation of the Geometallurgical model is a vital step in the model development and the design of the plant. Using adequate sampling and testing methods in a timely way allows early procurement and minimizes project risk. When placed in the Mine Block Model the data collected from these samples is often used to represent many thousands of tonnes of ore, so careful selection of the sample is essential to the success of the project as shown by several studies [2-3]. A well-considered test work program is one where the ore has been divided into zones with similar processing characteristics (e.g., grain size, hardness, and oxidation), and each zone has been separately sampled and tested. A key aspect of the ore characterization is understanding the amount of variation which can be expected in the processing characteristics of the ore across the entire ore deposit [4]. Ashley and Callow [5] give examples of problems that can occur when ore variability is not taken into account and of successful application of geometallurgy principles. As a minimum, several ore zone intersections should be tested and also the planned bench heights. It is recommended that the sampling be done to represent ore units that can be delivered to the mill in a given day. The selection of samples also needs to be focused on the first five years of ore in the mine plan. The conminution and flotation tests require considerable mass of sample. In practice core samples may be combined to create a composite sample which contains sufficient mass for the test. In most cases, the samples for geometallurgical testing come from diamond drill core so there is a limited amount available. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 175 Compositing samples together is not recommended but if necessary should be done with extreme caution, as the results produced will indicate some average condition which may not be representative of any particular ore fed to the processing plant during mine life, as well as smoothing/blending out the inherent variability of a deposit. Other problems that can occur when assessing the local variability of metallurgical variables in composite samples, is that the spatial loca

tion is lost, or the samples are not at constant support [3]. If composite samples must be created it is important that geologists, mining engineers and metallurgists are involved in the selection process. In particular, the metallurgist conducting the testing must understand the impact the use of this composite sample has on the applicability of the results to plant design or production forecasting. Otherwise the plant design will not achieve the required throughput because the “average” feed represented by the composite could be a blend that would never occur during the life of the mine [5]. If this occurs, a considerable mistake could be incurred and could have been avoided by adequate communication at the composite sample creation stage. 

Depending on the type of test work planned, the sample mass required can be as high as a hundred or more tonnes. There are several means of obtaining bulk samples such as trenching, driving adits, drilling large diameter core, all of which are expensive.  The method chosen is often controlled by the cost and the technical difficulty of accessing the ore body. An important point to note in the use of bulk sample is that the larger sample mass does not necessarily make the sample more representative of the ore body than small-diameter drill core samples. This is particularly true if the bulk sample is collected from one sampling point, as it will provide detailed information about that region of the ore body but does not account for any variation across the entire ore body. When a bulk sample is selected, the metallurgist must understand how the characteristics of that sample relate to the range of characteristics exhibited by the entire ore body. 

### **Diamond Drill Core** 

Diamond drill core is the usual means of obtaining samples of ore in areas where mining has not commenced or further mine recognition. Drill core is available in a range of diameters with the most common core for metallurgical testing being NQ (48 mm diameter). The choice of this core size is a balance between the cost of drilling and the need for as much material mass as possible for ore characterization. PQ core (85 mm diameter) is occasionally used where larger masses of sample are required, for example for JK Drop Weight Tests, pilot plant testing, etc. but this is the exception rather than the rule. Usually twin holes are drilled in selected cases, with the initial NQ hole (used for resource estimation assays, preliminary test work and ore variability assessments) being twinned with a second hole at HQ (64 mm diameter) or PQ size. The twinned hole provides a greater mass of material for detailed testing of the comminution, separation and geotechnical characteristics of the ore. 

A focus on core-based small-volume geometallurgical sampling provides a number of advantages. Drill core generally represents the most systematic view of an ore deposit and lies within the geologist’s domain. Any new geometallurgical technologies applied

## **GEOMETALLURGICAL CHARACTERIZATION** 

Many mining companies are now using geometallurgy to characterize the ore that will be treated in the concentrator when planning both greenfield and brownfield processing plants. The type of information required to design a process to treat an ore include: Grinding hardness; Grade and deportment of the valuable element(s) and deleterious elements; Mineralogy; Separation characteristics . 

The characterization of the variability starts with the selection of the samples to test the different ore type. This is based on the geology of the deposit, chemical analysis and physical characteristic of the ore. The selection of the samples also depends on the amount of sample required to do the tests. The design of a plant requires information on the following operational units: Comminution; Flotation; Sedimentation; Filtration; Mineral handling; Mineral transportation. 

Each of these operational units requires specific information to make the best design of the metallurgical plant. At the initial stage, laboratory scale tests are conducted. As the study progresses Pilot Plant tests are conducted to have information on a larger scale. 

## **Conminution** 

There are two main operations in mineral processing – liberation and separation. The liberation of minerals usually requires the ore to be broken into particles which contain high grade levels of the valuable mineral or minerals. Equally important for the determination of design parameters for primary crushing is the estimation of the granulometric distribution of the mineral that feed the primary crusher. 

The design approach to comminution has changed over the last 20 years, with the traditional circuit configuration of crusher – rod mill – ball mill circuits being replaced with concentrators with autogenous (AG) or semi-autogenous mills (SAG) – ball mill or HPGR – ball mill circuits. The tests designed to measure the comminution characteristics range from the early work Bond test for ball milling [6] through to the Drop Weight Test, SMC test [7] and SPI [8] and HPGR [9]. The tests normally used to determine specific energy consumption and therefore sizing equipment are mentioned below: 

- Traditional Circuit: Bond Crushing Work Index or Bond low energy impact test (primary crusher); Bond Rod Mill Work Index; Bond Ball Mill Work Index; Bond Abrasion Index Test. 

- SAG: Test SAG Power Index (SPI); Test de Starkey; Autogenous Abrasion Test; MacPherson Autogenous Wi Test – Awi, JK Drop Weight Test; SMC JK Test.

## **Concentration** 

First of all, laboratory tests are done to determine the parameters to carried out the flotation test to study the variability of copper extraction for all the main geological domains. The parameters determined are: Reagent Screening Tests; Optimum Grinding Test - P80; Determination Natural pH; Lime Consumption Test; Flotation Kinetic Tests. 

Once this is carried out, rougher flotation tests are conducted with samples of the geological domains to determine the impact of the geology in the recovery of the main elements. Laboratory-scale batch flotation provides a means to compare the flotation performance of the ore where only a few kilograms of sample are available. 

Secondly, the concentration grade is required to assess, therefore the following tests are done for this purpose together with sedimentation and filtration tests: Closed Circuit Flotation Test; Open Circuit Flotation Test; Sedimentation tests  of Concentrate and Tails; Concentrate filtration tests. 

## **Mineral Handling** 

Material testing is critical for successful delivery of an engineered solution for the bulk solids handling of the ore and concentrate. The system designs must be based on relevant material characteristics such us; granulometric analysis; maximum size; moisture; particle shape; storage time at rest and under pressure; consolidation pressure (height of the silo, bin, hopper and/or stock pile); weather conditions; clays, talc and/or additives content; chemical nature of the ore lithological and mineralogical. Common tests include: Fluidization tests; Cohesive strength; Compressibility and bulk density; Wall friction; Chute tests; Surcharge angle. 

## **Ore Mineral Characterization** 

Much of the non-grade information derived from drill core is a function of visual inspection as part of geological and geotechnical logging. The visual inspection includes map logging of minerals that suit the ore body. Industry clearly identified this process as a major weak link. Visual logging is generally highly subjective, experience-based, often conducted by junior personnel, and is difficult to support given the current trend to de-skilling in the industry. Many of the geological concepts and observations used in routine logging are 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

178 

typically related to exploration aspects and are not calibrated with or validated against processing performance. However, many of the interpretative lithologies introduced during routine geological logging have a tendency when combined with grade to become defi

nitive ‘ore types’. 

The effect of head grade on flotation concentrate has long been recognised by metallurgists, with an increase in head grade often leading to higher grade in the concentrate of this mineral. Another variable that affects the flotation behaviour is the textural characteristics of the ore and has a greater effect than changes in head grade. The mineralogy, grain size, shape, association and dispersion of grain of the minerals in an ore contribute to the ore texture, and are of fundamental importance in understanding the metallurgical behavior of the ore. The recovery and flotation rates of particles of a given size increase as the content of the particles increases. Gaudin [10] was one of the first to observe that locked particles float in some manner which is intermediate between fast floating free particles and non-floating particles of gangue. 

The mineral association is the measure of the amount of a mineral’s surface in contact with another mineral, and is used as an indicator of textural complexity. Another important factor is the mineral content of the intergrowth phases that would affect the interpretation of results as they tend to occur on the boundary between the two minerals, and will therefore affect the mineral association values. Fine-grained minerals which are intergrown and dispersed throughout a mineral matrix are more difficult to liberate than textures exhibiting massive characteristics [11]. Microscopic examination of particles is the only approach which can be used to quantify the particle composition of sulphide ores [12]. 

The flotation response of the particles depends upon particle composition (mineral distribution) and consistently across most size fractions [13] increased as the proportion of chalcopyrite in the particle increased. This pattern was observed consistently, as well as with other copper minerals (chalcopyrite, bornite, chalcocite), pyrite, gangue (all other minerals) It was also observed is that all the size fractions exhibited two component flotation characteristics indicating the presence of a fast-floating and a slow-floating component in the ore. The existence of this characteristic was not related to particle composition because this behaviour was observed for all composition classes including the fully liberated chalcopyrite. 

For comminution performance, information on bulk mineralogy (mainly gangue phases in low grade systems) and mesotextures at fairly low resolution are required to develop deterministic models. For liberation and recovery, a detailed microtextural understanding of the valuable phases and their immediate associations is required. Mesotextural information is relevant at the intact rock scale ranging from centimeters upward, while microtextural information typically involves comminuted feed and product at micron scale. The need for varying scales and resolutions represents a major challenge to providing systematic mineralogical information for geometallurgical

application. 

Recently, major mining companies have been using automated mineralogy systems to characterize their ore as a way of managing risk. Some of these organizations are using the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

179 

automated mineralogy systems to assess the mineralogy and textural characteristics of ores and their impact on the design parameters but unfortunately this work is seen as commercially sensitive and very little has been published about the work carried out. 

## **Testing Requirement** 

When the data is included in the block model of the ore body, the assays form the most detailed data set, with other analyses and tests being performed at much lower density. Some typical values for assays vs. metallurgical tests are provided by Williams and Richardson [2] are listed below, but these numbers depend on the geological characteristics of the ore: Assays >>10000; Mineralogy >1000; Comminution 100 – 300; Metallurgical tests (e.g. flotation, leaching) 100 – 300. The data presented above indicates that while detailed information can be obtained on the variation in the grade across the ore body, the same level of understanding is not obtained about the variation in comminution and separation characteristics. The reason for other tests such as flotation tests and grinding tests being performed at lower density is twofold: Firstly, these tests often require more sample mass than is available (from 1 to 2 m lengths of quarter core); and secondly, these tests cost considerably more than assays for mass requirement. 

To overcome these problems, MinnovEX has worked with industry sponsors to develop their approach, which uses a 4kg sample for their suite of tests [14]. The range of tests which MinnovEX can perform on the 4kg sample include their SAG Power Index (SPI) method for SAG milling characteristics, a modified Bond test for ball milling characteristics and the MinnovEX Flotation Test (MFT) for flotation characteristics. MinnovEX has also developed FLEET to estimate the final concentrate grade and recovery. JKMRC has also produced a laboratory batch flotation test to calculate a Flotability Index (FI). The FI has been validated for a copper ore in a Flotation Plant using two types of geological domain of a mine: the latter to calibrate the model while the former to validate it.  However, one weakness of this approach is that the flotability changes as other reagents are added, as well as when regrinding occurs within the flotation circuit. 

## **Quality Assurance and Quality Control** 

It is interesting to note that significant effort goes into the collection of core-scale grade involving careful sample preparation, use of reputable commercial laboratories, application of QA/QC and commitment to support costs commensurate with the importance of the results. Similar efforts and investment should go into the collection of core-based geometallurgical parameters that also have direct bearing on economic performance. T

herefore QA/QC should also be carried out in all the procedures for metallurgical testing. 

## **GEOMETALLURGICAL MODELLING** 

The primary aim of geometallurgy is to provide constrained inputs that reflect inherent geological variability and its impact on metallurgical performance. This requires quantification of ore deposits in terms of machine-based process parameters such as hardness, 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

180 

comminution energy, size reduction, liberation potential and product recovery. These parameters are used to populate deposit-scale block models, most typically through the application of geostatistics. Incorporation of geometallurgical parameters into resource modelling supplements traditional geology and grade-based attributes, enabling a more holistic approach to economic optimization of mineral production. Sophisticated geometallurgical block models can be used to predict and optimize economic attributes such as throughput, grade, grind size and recovery. However, other aspects that geometallurgical modeling of the metallurgical variables encounters when assessing the local variability are: 

- Generally samples are not at constant support; 

- A reasonable number of samples for the tests is difficult to obtain. Generally, the number of available samples is not sufficient to do a proper assessment; 

- Composite samples combining several increments from different places (resulting in a loss of spatial location) are used to get enough weight to perform metallurgical tests; . 

- Metallurgical recovery is not additive so the assessment of its spatial variability is not direct; 

- The spatial models of the geological variables which control the metallurgical behavior, such as lithology, alteration, mineralogy, texture. liberation factor, surface properties and ore zones, are not always available and should be taken into account; and 

- The scale process to forecast results from in situ simulated or estimated point values is not well known [3]. 

The trend towards larger numbers of more representative geometallurgical samples partly overcomes some of these problems, particularly the potential assessment of additivity and linearity through the use of cross-validation. However, effective extrapolation of geometallurgical processing performance attributes to the deposit scale requires a suite of statistical and population modelling techniques in addition to classical geostatistics. Predicting downstream metallurgical performance has become an increasingly important aspect of mineral processing operations. Ore petrology will fundamentally determine the types of metallurgical processes employed for ore treatment, their operational efficiency and the nature of processing problems encountered. It is based upon taking a geologically informed selection of test samples to determine metallurgical performance with the purpose of understanding the distribution of variables throughout an orebody, using accepted geostati

stical techniques to support metallurgical process modelling. 

The ultimate aim of geometallurgy is to replace geological domains or unconstrained ‘ore types’ with processing domains. These may or may not coincide with geological boundaries and different processing domains may not show common boundaries. Processing domains are also likely to be correlated with numeric performance such as throughput and recovery rather than categorical boundaries. In this respect they would share many aspects with grade. The overall methodology generates an estimate of mineral and elemental recovery for each ore sample that can be used as an input in geometallurgical models of the ore deposit. The stages in the overall methodology are: 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

181 

- Statistical data analysis of the metallurgical variables based on the metallurgical tests. This analysis would integrate large and complex geological and metallurgical databases to identify intrinsic attributes that affect mineral processing. This understanding would then be used to map the metallurgical response across a deposit. 

- Determination of deterministic modelling of processing attributes to identify intrinsic rock-based controls on metallurgical response. This is done through a multivariate process that includes class-based analysis, principal component analysis and of course modelling. Classes are multivariate assemblages of samples sharing similar intrinsic characteristics such as mineralogy, texture or structure. 

- Scale up to process output based on the needs where necessary. 

Classes may or may not coincide with traditional boundary definitions such as geology or alteration. Class-based analysis facilitates predictive modelling of processing indices by developing discrete class-based models. Results show class-based modelling provides more effective predictive capabilities when compared with universal models and enables robust predictions of processing performance attributes to be made. This is critical for providing the data support necessary for geostatistical modelling of geometallurgical attributes. A trend analysis procedure is applied to class-based modelling predictions to develop processing domains suitable for geostatistical application using currently available techniques. The integrated method incorporates a range of established mathematical and statistical techniques including Principal Component Analysis, Multiple Linear and Non-Linear Regression Modelling, and Cumulative Summation Analysis (cusum). 

If the analysis is carried on and implemented, the outcomes of geometallurgical modelling will enable effective management of project risk through robust deposit characterization, documenting variability within an orebody and, quantifying the impact of intrinsic variability on processing performance.

## **ABSTRACT** 

Optimization of copper concentrators has, traditionally, been hampered by lack of quantitative mineralogical data.  The

- The sulfides in aged stockpile ores and/or ores with extensive alteration may show significant tarnishing which results in sluggish float kinetics. Though aging can often be counteracted via increases of collector dosages in the roughers.

- Oxide copper minerals increase both pyrite and sphalerite activation.

- Self-floating minerals (such as talc, pyrophyllite, graphite, sericitic mica, serpentine) cause entrainment, agglomerations and increase of insol into concentrates.

4. Clay impacts reagent consumption and classification efficiency.

## **ABSTRACT** 

The present work describes a methodology for the analysis and modelling of geometallurgical units. The development of this study was based on exploration data mainly collected in the course of reverse circulation campaigns and previously mined areas found in strata-bound deposits located in northern Chile. 

From a methodology perspective, this study has been designed in several stages. The purpose of the first of these stages is to approximate reality by focusing the efforts on the modelization of the units to be incorporated into a long-term planning. Each of the selected variables has been determined by both linear and non-linear geostatistical methods. 

Finally, the results have been merged into a spatial block model applicable to the mine planning stage. 

**Key words** : Geometallurgical, ordinary kriging, indicator kriging, long-term planning, strata-bound deposits.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

This work was conducted in a mining company currently mining a copper stratabound deposit located in the north of Chile. 

This initiative was designed with the main purpose of incorporating into the longterm block model a number of geometallurgical variables (GMM) that may have some significance on such planning horizon, especially in acid-consumption and metallurgical recovery aspects.

## **THE GEOMETALLURGICAL CONCEPT** 

Studies of a mine’s life-cycle evolution clearly reveal the existence of a strong variability in contents, metallurgical recovery, acid consumption, etc. Some “families” of 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

205 

geological characteristics linked to similar metallurgical features can be

associated to these variations. 

Basically, the “geometallurgical model” can be defined as a spatial representation of the behaviour exhibited by the different geological units in the mineral valuation process to be assigned for treatment either by concentration or by leaching. 

Full knowledge of the ore deposit will allow defining what the actual value of the mineral is in terms of final throughput and its production costs in order to fully define the mine plan. By identifying the types of material, their spatial associations, and treatment variables, we can enhance mining operations planning and production. Better knowledge translates into less uncertainty and a lesser need to modify the mining plans in the event of unexpected occurrences. 

A GMM block can be described as a three-dimensional portion of a deposit ore characterized on the basis of its different geological and metallurgical properties. Based on this data, a complete record of the deposit can be created so that both its metallurgical performance and economic value can be accurately defined before the ore is transported to the metallurgical plant. 

The above entails an on-going and evolutionary work in time. In the particular case to be analysed here, the model construction will be focused on the variables to be defined as relevant at some point in time. 

## **APPLICATION OF THE GEOMETALLURGICAL CONCEPT** 

When dealing with this type of deposit where most of the information has been collected from reverse circulation drillings and old underground mine operations, consideration should be given to the fact that the fluctuations occurring in the results of the qualitatively-defined variables somehow lose the sense of invariability that might be granted to a point in space, but keep it in a general sense where that point and its properties are located. 

With regard to the specific case of the mine we are about to analyse, the focus will be placed on running a correlation between the geological variables; basically, lithology, mineralization, and metallurgical variables: recovery and reagent consumption. Based on these grounds, the definition of geometallurgical units will be proposed. 

Generally, a GMM model results from the interaction between the variables defined as the input variables and the response variables. In a GMM model, the responses obtained in the leaching process allow the possibility of predicting the type of behaviour the unit will display the moment it enters into the process. Therefore, an adequate representation of both geological and metallurgical characteristics will be a key condition to obtain accurate final results, even in an average characteristic behaviour, and to attempt to quantify the impact those variables can have on the mine planning model.

## **MULTIVARIATE SPATIAL DEFINITION OF GEOLOGICAL DOMAINS FOR  GRAMALOTE GOLD DEPOSIT** 

Sandy Prieto Ili*, Luis Valencia _SGS Minerals S.A. Chile_ Juen Velez, Juan Arbelбez, _SGS Colombia S.A._ 

Claudio Devaux, Pablo Noriega & Fernando Arredondo, _Gramalote Colombia Ltd._ 

## **ABSTRACT** 

As part of its prefeasibility study, a “Spatial Definition of Multivariate Domains” was completed at Gramalote gold deposit with the purpose of conducting a proper geometallurgical sample collection process, where each sample set must exhibit different geological and chemical characteristics. The domains were defined by applying geological, geophysical, and chemical variables by means of a principal components factor analysis and, later on, a cluster analysis. 

The statistical analysis was carried out with a data set containing 3

8,295 entries and involving a univariate, bivariate and multivariate analysis framework based on data mining techniques. As to the multivariate analysis, this was mainly developed through the principal components factor analysis, where the variables to be used in the cluster analysis were identified. In all, thirteen categorical variables were employed (including lithology, types of structures, alteration, occurrence and intensity of the alteration, among others) and thirty three continuous variables (such as fire assay, ICP and magnetic susceptibility) during the different analysis stages. 

The univariate and bivariate statistical analysis led to the conclusion that, apart from the conventional results, the elements _As_ , _Sb_ , _Th_ and _U_ are different in two populations whose origin can be associated to the use of different detection limits in the analysis since the chemical analysis were conducted in two different laboratories. 

The analysis of scatter matrices revealed that no bivariate relationships exist with gold grades and, consequently, multivariate analysis had to be applied. The cluster 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

218 

analysis allowed the identification of 5 domains where an inversely proportional relationship exists between the gold grade and the size of domains. The elements that helped define the five domains are occurrence of the alteration, potassium, sodium, copper, gold, and sulphur. These clusters represent domains of geometallurgical validity since each of them offers robustness in terms of spatial continuity which was checked simultaneously with the multivariate analysis. 

Domain 1 displays a continuity limited to the center area of the deposit, with more or less 60% of low-intensity, quartz-sericitic alteration hosted in the fractures with an average 0.18g/t of gold contents. A little more than 20% of the data sets for this domain showed a certain type of potassic alteration; a little less than 20% of the elements pertaining to this domain showed a carbonate sericitic alteration. The rest of domain 1 samples present supergene argillic alterations. 

The remaining domains can be characterized also based on the type of alteration. For example, it was verified that domain 2 is represented by smaller volumes, scattered but restricted to the highest average gold-bearing zone (2.43 g/t) and of, predominantly, moderate-intensity potassium alterations, hosted in veinlets. 

Domain 3 is widely scattered across the ore deposit and is consistent with the volumes of alteration-free rock waste. Nearly 100% of domain 3 samples do not present alterations; that is, the cluster method successfully identified all alteration-free samples as pieces pertaining to the same set of samples. Thus, domain 3 is fully defined by means of the alteration; thus, it can be concluded that all samples without any alteration can be defined as pertaining to domain 3. 

Domain 4 is scattered all over the ore deposit though restrict

ed to the high area characterized by a strong and penetrating clayey alteration. In the center area, this domain becomes deeper and characterized by highly modified rocks; however, as a general occurrence, this deepening is associated to the shearing of NNW-SSE-oriented faults. As to samples with pervasive alteration, nearly all of them were found under domain 4. That feature defines the domain. 

Finally, domain 5 continuity is restricted to the center area of the ore deposit and envelope, directly in the high-grade zone (domain 2). This domain stretches to the east in a discontinuous pattern due to the presence of some NNW-SSE-oriented faults, where this discontinuity becomes covered by waste rock (domain 3). The rocks pertaining to this domain exhibit a strong veinlet-hosted, quartz-sericitic alteration. 

The spatial distribution of the statistically defined domains was characterized by a concentric structure where the volume shrinks from the outer rims to the center, as opposed to grade distribution that becomes higher as it approaches the center of the ore deposit. There is also a clear definition of the most superficial zone corresponding to the saprolite lithology type. 

This work shows the methodology applied in the search of domains from a mathematical-statistical and geological point of view, as well as the characterizations specific to each domain identified with this methodology.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

This work is inscribed within the Gramalote project, undertaken by Compaснa Minera Anglo Gold Ashanti Colombia S.A., which commissioned SGS Minerals Services the development of a study related to SGS geometallurgical framework. This is a 6-stage study. Stage 1 involves SGS geometallurgical framework which is the Multivariate Spatial Definition of Geological Domains. 

SGS geometallurgical framework consists of a methodology intended to add value to mining projects and operations, with due consideration of a number of uncertainty sources. This framework consists of a technological platform comprising geological, mining, metallurgical, geochemical, textural, environmental, etc. aspects as key components to the mining development process. 

This work is aimed at defining the spatial domains (or geological units) existing in the Gramalote gold deposit that exhibit both similar geological, geochemical, mineralogical, and textural characteristics as well as adequate spatial continuity. 

## **BACKGROUND** 

On a first stage, Anglo Gold Ashanti “Gramalote Project” made all the project’s geological and metallurgical information available to its professional staff and SGS in order to study the material thoroughly and identify the opportunities for the project’s development phase.

## **DOMAIN DEFINITION METHODOLOGY** 

The methodology applied to generate domains is known as the cluster methodology. The cluster analysis can be found within the series of analysis offered by data mining techniques. It is associated to group identification or pattern search tasks in large data sets where measurements made of a large number of variables for each observation or object are contained, as are the data sets for the project under development. This methodology assumes that different sub-populations exist within the population being studied and, with the help of an iterative method, this methodology attempts to discover these sub-populations. 

Patterns are searched through groups of multivariate observations within the clusters (or groups). The purpose of this methodology is to detect an optimal grouping so that the observations or objects within each cluster are similar but clusters are dissimilar

## to each other. 

This is the exact objective pursued by generating Gramalote deposit’s domains and this is why this methodology was chosen. In this case, composite groupings in clusters will be sought, such that the composites pertaining to the same cluster or group are as similar as possible in terms of variables of interest (grade, mineralization, alteration, etc.) and as dissimilar as possible from composites pertaining to each one of the other clusters. Thus, groups or domains will be generated with similar geological characteristics which is precisely the objective pursued in this stage. 

This analysis is expected to discover natural groupings in the data sets; that is, groupings that are meaningful to Gramalote’s geological research and such domains can be used as the basis of new undertakings such as, for example, sample selection for metallurgical processes.

## **PRINCIPAL COMPONENTS FACTOR ANALYSIS** 

The main purpose of the principal component analysis, also known by its acronym PCA, is to reduce the dimensionality of the problem. This can be very useful when large data sets are being handled, with a large number of variables and that number must be reduced since there is no full certainty as to how relevant each of these variables is in explaining variability; that is, the number of variables capable of explaining the variability of the entire data set must be reduced. 

The above can be found within the type of analysis called “analysis of factors” or “factor analysis”, capable of detecting clusters of variables with similar behavior or some underlying structures in data sets which descriptive univariate and bivariate analysis are unable to detect because they do not consider the interaction of two or more variables at the same time. 

The first step to take in a principal component analysis is a hypothesis test in order to assess the suitability of the analysis for these data sets. This allows quantifying what percentage of the total variability of the data set can be successfully explained when the dimensionality of the problem is reduced by factor analysis and, therefore, what percentage of information is lost. On each new step, the principal components factor analysis runs hypothesis tests to evaluate the suitability of the analysis for that particular data set. 

During this principal components factor analysis, 8 components were identified which, in all, explain 66.99% of the total variability exhibited by the deposit’s data set. This can be considered as good level of variance explained with minimum information lost. 

With these results at hand, the variables that define each component are examined in order to accurately define what information corresponds to each individual component. 

In this case, the gold grade variable ( _Au_ ) was proved to appear in the third component. In that same component, variables _Cu_ , _K_ , _Na_ , and _S_ were also found. However, each component can be analyzed to account for the variability of all variables and, at the same time, use all the obtained components in order to explain la variability of the entire ore deposit. ## **CONCLUSIONS** 

Univariate and bivariate statistical analysis have established that elements _As_ , _Sb_ , _Th_ and _U_ are different from each other in two populations whose origin is associated to the use of different detection limits in the analysis. This proves true in the relationship they keep with _lab_analisis_ , the variable that indicates the place (and method) where the chemical analysis were conducted. 

The analysis of scatter matrices leads to the conclusion that no bivariate relationships exist with gold grades; thus, multivariate analysis must be used. 

The results of the statistical tests derived from the principal components factor analysis indicate the existence of relationships between the variables. This allowed the definition of 8 components which would account for 66 _._ 99%, in total, of the variance of data sets as a whole. 

A number of relatio

nships were identified in some of the components which account for known phenomena of expected occurrence inside the deposit; for example, the component where _Au_ and _Cu_ (in chalcopyrite) are related to _S_ (in pyrite); the component that links magnetic susceptibility with _Ti_ (likely presence of titanite); the component where the variable “type of analysis” (associated to different detection limits) is related to the elements divided into two statistical populations ( _As_ , _Sb_ , _Th_ and _U_ ); and the component that relates _K_ and _Na_ with the type, occurrence and intensity of the alteration. 

The cluster analysis helped identify 5 domains where an inversely proportional relationship exists between the gold grade and the size of domains. Nearly 60% of domain 1 presents a quartz-sericitic alteration; a little more than 20% of the information contained in this cluster reveals some type of potassic alteration; a little less than 20% of the elements pertaining to this cluster display carbonate-sericitic alterations. The rest of the samples from cluster 1 presents supergene argillic alterations. In like manner, the remaining domains can be characterized according to their type of alterations. For example, it is clear that 100% of the samples from domain 3 are free from alterations. As to samples with pervasive alterations, almost all of them can be found under domain 4 and this is the occurrence that defines the domain. 

The spatial distribution of the statistically defined domains is known to be concentric where the volume shrinks from the outer rims towards the center, as opposed to grade distribution which increases towards the center of the deposit. The most superficial zone, of saprolite lithology type, is clearly defined and represented in green in the spatial model. 

These geological domains, obtained through the cluster methodology, can be updated by adding new samples in the analysis. However, this one is ready to be used as a geological model for future analysis.

## **ABSTRACT** 

Increasing global copper demand and tightening energy, water, and environmental constraints in the face of continuously declining copper grades create an increasing pressure for innovation in copper mining. Highly disseminated, inhomogeneous, and refractive ores give copper mining the most challenging, diverse, and fluctuating feeds in any process industry. Our geometallurgical modeling must accurately reflect the geology and geochemistry to faithfully guide and constrain our process innovation to best fit our ore bodies. 

Historical grade-tonnage relations indicate that a fractal distribution accurately describes the spatial distribution of copper in most of our copper deposits. This has implications a

nd places constraints on the degree and means of pre-concentration enrichment.  Quantitative differences in the measured fractal dimension describing copper and silver deposits are seen to create qualitatively different requirements for their efficient mining and processing. Extrapolating from historical copper grade-tonnage data indicates that gangue enrichment by sorting could double world copper reserves.
