## **THE PERSISTENCE OF CLUSTERING** 

Three trucks drive into a copper mine. They come out carrying the same ore tonnages but different amounts of copper. On average half the copper is concentrated into one truck, which carries double the grade of the other two. In silver mines every third ore truck is concentrated four-fold; carrying double the silver of the other two. What are we to conclude? That silver miners are sloppy and prone to dilution? No, both are equally skilled at mining above cut-off and avoiding dilution. The degree of concentration and clustering appears to be intrinsic to the ore. The same persistent pattern is seen across time, across grades, and across tonnages:  100 years ago every third donkey pulled twothirds the silver and half the copper. And it persists across deposits, districts and ore types: taking any three separated billion-ton copper deposits, typically half the total copper is found in the richest of those three. And the pattern persists across grade with three of nine ore trucks carrying half the copper and the richest one of those three carrying half their copper, or a quarter of the total copper in the nine. Similarly (but differently) for silver, one of nine trucks carries four-ninths (nearly half!) the silver, whether as a by-product or from a primary silver mine. 

The distribution of metal in ore reminds one of the distributions of wealth in societies. Copper is more disseminated with most of the copper in lower grades and (like mid-twentieth century America) half the wealth held in the richest third. Silver is more clustered, with the lower grades quite depleted and (like twenty-first century America) having two-thirds of the wealth held by the richest third.  This difference in distributions has implications for mining.  Silver and other precious metals are "top heavy" deposits with most of the precious metals concentrated in the higher grades whereas copper, even in the richest deposits, is mostly found in the lower grades. Extracting a portion of that wealth previously thought un-economic is the topic of this presentation. 

## **ORIGINS AND MEASUREMENT OF CLUSTERING** 

Copper has an average abundance in the continental crust of 25 parts per million [1]. A thousand-fold concentration can occur in the ore forming process. In a typical copper porphyry deposit a magma plume is forced upward under high pressure through cracks in overlying rock [2, 3]. Concentration of the fluid from near crustal abundance levels can occur by either of two mechanis

ms or their combination: chromatography and distillation [4-6]. In distillation, the melt is progressively enriched in elements excluded from the solidifying minerals. This is especially common in non-mineral forming elements such as gold and can result in as much as a million-fold concentration from their part-per-billion level crustal abundances. Copper and other base metals have a richer range of co-ordination complexes and can form minerals with a host of common elements such as sulfur and iron making up the magma. This causes most of the copper to crystallize in the minerals of the solid phase while most of the precious metals stay in the melt for further concentration. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

231 

This enrichment process creates a deposit trending to increasing grade upward in the direction of plume travel. The deposit is left behind the rising enrichment front. In a single large deposit the depleted zones are not further enriched nor further depleted, they are solidified. The resulting deposit is very asymmetric, with enriched portions further enriched and progressively higher grades occupying progressively smaller tonnages. This reflects the one-way nature of the solidification process, the depleted solid is neither further enriched nor depleted but the enriched melt can be further enriched before precipitation as a solid. This gives rise to a grade tonnage distribution that is neither a symmetric Gaussian, bell-shaped curve, nor a log-normal distribution, but one skewed more severely toward higher grades and described by a power law. We can derive this power law grade-tonnage distribution by noting that at the precipitation front an increment of metal mass lost by the solid, ds, is gained by the magma, dm. The precipitation/melt front in the rising hydrothermal plume is like a push-broom sweeping the metal into the melt, more effectively for precious than for base metals. For an increment of enrichment, the fractional increase of metal moving into the melt, dm/m is proportional to the fractional increase in enriched ore tonnage created, 



Where the constant of proportionality, k, is the partition coefficient, a measure of the degree of partitioning or fractionation into the melt [6]. If k = 0, then dm = 0 and no metal is lost from the melt into the solid. The solid is swept clean and the melt is successively concentrated resulting in a nugget at the top of the deposit and average crustal abundances below. In the opposite extreme, k=1, all of the metal is lost into the solid, the fractional increment in ore tonnage equals the incremental loss in the melt. There is therefore no fractionation or concentration across the melt/solid interface, no enrichment, the deposit is homogenous, of constant grade from top to bottom. For silver, historical mine production data [7] described below indicates that kAg=1/3. This means most of the silver is excluded from the solid and concentrated into the melt. For copper, the sam

e data indicate kCu=2/3. Most of the copper goes into the solid from the melt, with the melt more rapidly depleted with rise, putting most of the copper into the lower grades. We can find an expression for metal concentration across the deposit by integrating Equation 1 from the bottom of the deposit to the top, 



From Equation 2 we see that in a copper deposit (k=2/3) one quarter of the metal (M/Mo=1/4) is concentrated in one eighth of the ore tonnage (T/To=1/8), whereas for silver (k=1/3) the richest eighth of the tonnage (T/To=1/8) contains fully half the metal (M/Mo=1/2). To extract half the copper from a deposit we have to mine not one-eighth but about one-third (T/To= (1/2)<sup>3/2</sup> = 0.35) of the tonnage. 

The same distribution of copper across tonnage can result from a chromatographic enrichment process rather than distillation. Here the copper bearing magmatic fluid is forced through a highly fragmented medium. The copper mineral is

In a single ore forming event this results in the same asymmetric deposit of Equation 2. Once material finds its final precipitation spot it is not further concentrated nor diluted. Multiple hydrothermal ore forming events with different pressure and temperature conditions can give rise to different fractionation coefficients, k, resulting in a multiple slopes of the grade vs. tonnage plot [4]. Mixing of a deposit either during or subsequent to the primary ore forming process can further concentrate low grade portions of the deposit and dilute high grade portions producing a grade tonnage curve no longer rising toward greatest concentrations in the least tonnages but peaking at mid grades due to the repeated concentration of low grades and depletion of high grades. Figure 2- Fraction of copper gangue concentrated to cutoff grade by sorting This self-similar scaling property characteristic of power laws such as equations 2 and 3 is the signature of a fractal relation [12, 13]. Grade-tonnage relations are an example of a self-similar, fractal scaling, as was first pointed out in 1986 in a classic paper by Don Turcotte, Dean of American Geologists [14]. A fractal dimension is the _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 235 exponent in a power law relation that connects two fundamentally disparate entities; number (as in the number of copper atoms) and dimension (as in length or time). The "Fractal Dimension" has been made popular with examples of a purely geometrical nature, for instance relating the length of a coastline, L, with the number of rulers of length l placed end to end to used measure it [13]. The number of rulers N, increases as the ruler length decreases, as N = A/ l1.2 resulting in the measured length of the coa

st L=Nl = A/l0.2 increasing here as the inverse fifth root of ruler length. The smaller the ruler, the more fit in the nooks and crannies to measure a longer coastline. This power dependence is evidence of a self-similar scaling between the two lengths involved - the roughness of the coastline looks the same over a range of magnifications. The magnitude of the exponent increases with roughness and characterizes that roughness. While interesting and easier to visualize than grade-tonnage relations, this is perhaps not that surprising, representing as it does, a synthetic and purely geometrical relation between two lengths. Yet even in this simplest of fractal applications our modeling accuracy has improved: the distribution of peak-heights on a rough surface is not Gaussian as previously thought but fractal. This has deepened our understanding and greatly improved the accuracy of our modeling of not only roughness, but phenomenon previously thought un-model-able such as fracture, earthquakes, and stock market crashes and now possibly nugget appearances and grade-tonnage relations in mining [12]. From Equation 2 we can obtain an equation relating number and dimension by noting that M is proportional to the number of copper atoms contained in the tonnage, T, and can be written as the ore density times its volume which scales as the cube of a linear distance L, This identifies the fractal dimension, D, with the fractionation coefficient, D=3k. With this definition the fractal dimension D, is three in the limit of a homogenous distribution, two for copper, one for silver, and drops to zero in the limit of extreme clustering where all the metal is concentrated in a single nugget. This greater clustering of precious over base metals was manifest spatially across the deposit as well as historically in accumulated production data. Single exponent power law decay down to crustal abundances is not observed. As Allegre and Lewin explain in their paper, [4] single exponent behavior occurs over a limited range of tonnages or length scales in a limited set of ore forming processes. If post-deposition weathering and concentration are present, a multi-exponent (multifractal) or binomial distribution giving rise to a log-normal grade tonnage distribution may more accurately describe the deposit. The log-normal distribution has remained the traditional description of grade-tonnage relations although it has been pointed out that it does not fit the data at large tonnages as well as the power law, fractal model [8]. While the exponent of the grade-tonnage power law is best determined by measurement from core assays, these disparate observations can be reconciled by noting that single power law behavior can be expected in the modeling of massive sulphide deposits but is not expected to be an accurate model either outside of the main hydrothermal ore-forming plume nor in the weathered oxide altered zone above it. Given that the portion of the deposit where the fractal model may be most applicable is in the massive sulphides now holding two-thirds of the world's copper reserve, it makes sense to use that model to explore the possibility of concentrating the ore, to effectively enlarge that reserve. This is where we turn our attention now. 

## **DOUBLING THE COPPER RESERVE** 

Equation 3 relates the average grade of the accumulated tonnage mined. To find the grade currently being mined we can differentiate Equation 2 to connect the instantaneous grade being mined, dM/dT, to the integral values M/T: C' = dM/dT = kM/T = kC. For copper the instantaneous grade, C' = 2C/3 is two-thirds of the average grade. If we take C' as our economic mill cut-off grade and ask the question for the block of waste between C' and C'/2 (containing three times the copper (3M) in seven times the tonnage (7T) as found above cutoff) how much enrichment do we need to bring a portion of that from its average grade, 3M/7T (= 3C/7 = 3(3C'/2)/7 = 9C'/14), up to cut off grade, C'?  The enrichment required is the ratio of the cutoff to the average grade, 14/9 = 1.55 ((2C/3)/(3C/7) = 14/9 = 1.

55). Knowing that the material below cut-off is very inhomogeneous in grade, it's natural to wonder what fraction of that below cut-off tonnage is in pockets that are already enriched 55% over the average. Perhaps surprisingly, Equation 3 can give us the answer: T/To = (C/Co)<sup>(1/(k-1))</sup> = (9/14)<sup>3</sup> = .26. From Equation 2 we see that 41% of the copper (=(9/14)<sup>2</sup> ) contained in this 26% of the waste tonnage is actually ore, already enriched above cutoff grade, existing in pockets and just waiting to be parsed out. Note that this is 24% (3M (9/14)<sup>2</sup> =1.24M) more copper than was found above cutoff, so if this copper can be economically sorted out of the waste then the reserve has been effectively increased by 124% - we've more than doubled the reserve. In Table 2, below we see that to double the copper reserve we need to sort through four times the waste tonnage or 32 times the tonnage for silver.

But if you were to enrich by sorting out the pockets of high grade from low grade material how fine would you have to sort? One ton scoops, a kilo-ton, a kilogram, a milligram? Certainly if you grind to mineral release you can get more than 41 percent of the metal out but how much can you get from run of mine ore, crushed to convey? We can address that by imagining a meter diameter core drilled through the deposit and laid down intact on a conveyor. If we ask how fast on average does the grade move away from the cutoff value on the conveyor or in the mine then we are interested in the variogram, or autocorrelation of the grade, 



Here we find that the copper and silver ores are qualitatively different. As has been pointed out [6, 12, 13] for ores having a fractal dimension less than 1.5 (such as silver) the variogram is anti-persistent, varying wildly with no persistent trends.  For fractal dimension greater than 1.5, such as copper, the variogram has persistent long term trends in grade. The number of cut-off grade crossings is greatly reduced for persistent trending deposits such as copper, allowing the sorting to be done in copper accurately with many fewer misclassifications than expected concentrating a silver deposit. We find that grade makes a random walk called Fractional Brownian Motion [13] whose burstiness has been used to describe the density of internet traffic to the prices of commodities traded on international markets and has a decidedly non-Gaussian statistics due to the long range correlations that span the deposit, or the globe. Interestingly only uranium

ore deposits exhibited D=3/2 [7] and are therefore predicted to exhibit nontrending deposits with grade variations making a true Brownian motion characterized by a variogram that increases linearly in time and a grade-tonnage distribution following Gaussian statistics. 

Another way to express this is to look at the power spectrum of grade variations coming off the conveyor. The power spectrum is found from the Fourier Transform of

the grade autocorrelation or variogram [12, 13]. The resulting power spectrum varies as frequency to the (1-2D) power, f<sup>1-2D</sup> . Silver exhibits a classic flicker "one-over-f" spectrum as seen for instance in the intensity fluctuations of a campfire, and for much for the same reason. The campfire having a fuel whose caloric value was deposited with a fractionation coefficient comparable to the fractionation of silver out of the melt.  The fluctuations of copper grade coming off the conveyor exhibit a power spectrum whose frequency varies as one over frequency cubed, 1/f<sup>3</sup> [12]. This means that the high frequency components are highly attenuated compared to the wild, 1/f flicker of silver. Copper grade exhibits deliberate, persisting trends across the deposit and along the conveyor. This is consistent with the narrow vein nature of silver and the slower trending nature of copper deposits. In Table 1 above are shown the different power law exponents of the variogram and power spectrum for copper and silver deposits. Note that a certain amount of mixing and blending inevitably occurs in blasting, mining and crushing. This mixing is primarily over the shorter end of the spatial scales and so is not expected to dilute the pockets of enriched copper appreciably, although it may prevent silver enrichments from approaching their theoretical maximum presented here. From Table 2, above we see that if our goal is to recover as much copper from the waste as was found in the ore, one need only sort through four times the tonnage below cutoff as above. With silver thirty-two times as much waste needs to be mined as was ore, surely an onerous sorting task. If our goal is more modest, just to process as much enriched waste as we did ore, then we will find two-thirds the copper or one-third the silver as was found in their ores. As we stated at the start, the richest third of a copper deposit contains half the copper. This law is scale invariant, in both spatial and grade scaling, and holds true below cutoff in the waste, where the richest third of the waste is actually ore. The fractal nature of our chalcopyrite deposits reveals the key to doubling the copper reserve. 

## **COPPERGENESIS** 

That’s copper: the richest third of the deposit contains half the copper. Strangely, it seems it's always been that way, on earth and in the stars. Copper is doubly distinguished in the stellar nursery where all the elements were made from hydrogen in the early universe. It

is the lightest element not burned in the thermonuclear fusion reaction that powers the stars. It does not produce energy but absorbs it in an endothermic reaction that eventually quenches the star. Unlike the precious metals, copper is not produced in a super nova explosion in an instant. Instead it is baked in the star, forged from the atoms of life in the Carbon-Nitrogen-Oxygen thermonuclear fusion power cycle until concentrated slowly by neutron bombardment of iron in heavy massive stars, 10 to 50 times heavier than our sun [15]. The most massive third of these stars produced over half the copper in our galaxy. The buildup of this copper then quenched the stars' burning, causing its collapse, the subsequent supernova explosion distributing the copper around the early milky way galaxy, some of which condensed into our earth where inexorable processes continue to concentrate copper. Chile has the greatest concentration of both copper and astronomical observatories on Earth. Perhaps it's time to build another observatory, this one looking down, to reignite another era of selective mining of copper, first started ten thousand years ago in Chile.

## **ABSTRACT** 

Characterisation of copper samples by leaching tests is conducted frequently by a number of commercial laboratories. These leach tests not only have the potential to provide more sample information than is gathered routinely but furthermore, in investigations into these traditional laboratory leach analyses, it was found that the determination of copper mineralogical deportment is not as selective as is claimed. New leach protocols have therefore been developed by Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) researchers to improve the accuracy of calculated copper mineralogy (oxides, chrysocolla, chalcocite, covellite, bornite and chalcopyrite). The validation of results from leach tests, using quantitative mineralogical analysis, is essential for quality control. An accurate, robust statistical method for QEMSCAN (Quantitative Evaluation of Minerals by SCANning electron microscopy) data analysis and validation of the new proposed selective leaching approach was therefore developed. The development and improved accuracy of these diagnostic and selective leach tests, including the use of the QEMSCAN for validation, will be highlighted with examples of applications to real samples from three different operations.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

Routine characterisations of large batches of copper samples by leaching tests are conducted frequently by a number of commercial and site based laboratories. Information reported from such leaches on copper ores may include copper recoveries and mineralogical information such as water soluble, weak acid soluble, cyanide soluble and strong acid soluble copper content. 

More sample information than is gathered from routine leaches can be obtained with limited additional cost and effort and often simply by further interrogation of the data obtained. From literature searches and through our multiple collaborations, we are aware that a number of researchers, companies and their technical groups have developed methods that depend on i) the

use parallel analytical tests that incorporate quality assurance/quality control protocols, ii) recognition that leach results under varying leach conditions may include the partial leaching of minerals and/or iii) mathematical combinations of leach results to provide estimates of mineral content [1-8]. Researchers at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) have aimed to develop independent protocols to maximise the usefulness of traditional laboratory leaches, for example, for confirmation of copper deportment and information on reagent consumption, impurity deportment and solution speciation. These leaches have been termed “diagnostic leaches” and provide information for use in processing. 

In further research conducted at the CSIRO, traditional laboratory leaches for copper mineralogy predictions were tested using a statistically reliable comparison method. Leaches were often found to over- or under-predict copper oxides and primary and/or secondary copper sulfides causing the inferred mineralogical deportment and geochemical classification determined from the various leaches to differ markedly from the theoretical or assumed value. Based on this auditing work, test development and leach tests on samples from multiple sites resulted in a scheme to target copper oxides, chrysocolla, chalcocite, covellite, bornite and chalcopyrite. These leaches have been termed “selective leaches”. An accurate, robust statistical method for mineralogical data analysis was also developed to validate and improve results from the leach tests. 

In this paper, the diagnostic and selective leach tests are applied to samples from three different copper/gold and copper deposits. The results presented highlight the value of using the diagnostic leaches for obtaining additional useful information for processing and the selective leaches for a more accurate determination of copper mineralogy.

## **Diagnostic Leaching** 

Eighteen samples (25 g, P80 -100 µm) from a South American copper/gold deposit (termed Site A) were cyanide bottle roll leached (150 mL of 1.5 g L<sup>-1</sup> sodium cyanide solution, pH > 9.5) at ambient conditions and 200 rpm for 24 h and sulfuric acid bottle roll leached (150 mL of 5 % solution) at ambient conditions and 60 rpm for 1 h. Solution samples were analysed for Au, Cu and Fe by atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS, Varian SpectrAA-800). For the cyanide leaches, the concentrations of thiocyanate (SCN<sup>-</sup> ) and thiosulfate (S2O32-) were determined by high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) on a Waters 2695 HPLC. Mineral Liberation Analyser (MLA) data were provided by the site for the samples.

Calibration factors were obtained for the copper oxides, chrysocolla, chalcocite, bornite, covellite and chalcopyrite for each of the Site B and C samples. The calibration factors correct the original leach data and ensure that the slope of the copper concentration from mineralogy matches that from the leach data. It is important to note that mineralogical calibration factors developed for one site cannot be transferred to samples from a different deposit or ore zone. An example of a calibration plot obtained for the copper oxide minerals in the Site B samples is shown in Figure 3. Leaching and mineralogical results may differ because of inaccuracies in analysis in either technique or

The percent copper (by mass) per mineral from MLA (M) and from the selective leaching analysis (L) for the Site B and C sample calibration sets are shown in Figure 4. The maximum difference between copper predictions from the mineralogical

and CSIRO leach analysis is 2.2 and 0.2 mass percent copper, respectively. The developed leaching scheme appears to predict copper deportment well, but a more accurate prediction of bornite and covellite would improve the scheme greatly. Miscalculation of bornite and covellite concentrations occurs because of the overlap in percentages leached in the different chemical matrices (i.e. lower leach selectivity to these minerals), the complex leaching chemistry and number of intermediates that bornite can form, the relatively low concentrations of both minerals in the sample sets tested (covellite and bornite concentrations overall in both samples varied from 0.002–1.07 and 0.005–0.95 (with one sample of 2.13) mass % copper, respectively) and the low number of samples containing these minerals. Mineralogical analysis of additional residue samples and modification of the leaching conditions (more moderate or aggressive conditions using current reagents or more sensitive reagents) could improve the leaching predictions. Further analysis of leach residue samples by QEMSCAN is being conducted to refine the CSIRO leach calibration (especially to confirm extents of chrysocolla leaching and to reduce the copper “other” classification in the Site C leach results). 

Automated mineralogical techniques can produce highly reproducible, quantitative mineralogical results as well as quantify mineral abundances at low levels. However, QEMSCAN data are normalised to 100 % (unless mass flow data are entered) and therefore mineral abundances in residues may increase because of mass loss from the dissolution of certain minerals. This makes direct interpretation of mineral abundance 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

252 

changes based on the QEMSCAN data challenging. Furthermore, such a technique also requires the ability to distinguish significant mineralogical changes from background and sampling error. To address these difficulties, a robust statistical methodology was developed by the CSIRO for QEMSCAN analysis, data processing and interpretation of data from leach tests [16]. The following guidelines summarise the methodology used for transforming the data, comparing the minerals leached between ore and residue despite mass loss in the leaching process, and a statistical methodology for determining the magnitude, direction and significance of changes in mineral abundance after leaching. 

1. Conduct leach tests on the selected sample suite. 

2. Prepare and analyse at least two QEMSCAN mounts for each head and leach residue sample. An identical species identification protocol (SIP) file setup is required for all samples analysed. 

3. Normalise QEMSCAN data with respect to a mineral that remains unchanged during leaching. 

4. Calculate the mean abundances for each mineral in the head and residue samples, and the change in abundance (absolute and/or relative). 

5. Calculate a p-value based on Student’s t-distribution from the means and variances o

f each mineral in both the head and residue data sets. 

6. Choose a confidence level at which the mean is significant and determine the p- values which indicate significance at the chosen level. 

7. All differences with associated p-values smaller than or equal to the chosen value indicate a statistically significant change in mass during the leach. To determine the actual change, subtract the residue mean mass percentage from the head sample mass percentage for a particular mineral or calculate the percentage change in phase difference.

## **CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS** 

Value can be obtained from the detailed interrogation of diagnostic leaching results without requiring additional extensive leaching analysis. Mineralogical information may be used to supplement this analysis. For example, a simple check of kinetic behaviour and expected ratio of copper in solution (from the diagnostic leach) to major copper mineral in the sample (from mineralogical analysis) could provide useful confirmation of operating conditions, explanations for variations in expected recoveries and optimization of process conditions. Information in addition to that which is usually derived from traditional industrial diagnostic leaches may be of great benefit for improving processing parameters, r

educing costs and ensuring compliance with health and safety regulations. 

Modified selective leaching protocols were applied to over 100 samples from two deposits (a copper/gold and copper deposit) as a preliminary proof of principle test of the developed leaches and as a comparison to conventional laboratory leaching tests. The two main advantages of using the methodology proposed in the selective leaching test work are (i) that routine quantification of discrete copper-mineral phases can be obtained 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

without costly and possibly time-consuming mineralogical analysis and (ii) that more accurate copper mineralogy can be determined than may be obtained from standard literature procedures as applied commercially. The tailored reagent selection and data interpretation developed in this methodology allows for the more accurate quantification of mineral phases and the reduced likelihood of classification errors. The tests are also applied in parallel rather than sequentially thereby potentially reducing labour or time constraints and associated costs. To ensure confidence in the results, the application of a robust and statistically sound mineralogical analysis to a calibration set as developed by the CSIRO for QEMSCAN analysis is advised to calibrate and confirm leach results before their application to a large number of samples.

## **REDUCING PRODUCTION VARIABILITY IN SHORT TERM SCHEDULING – A PRACTICAL APPROACH** 

E. Madariaga, M. Grigaliunas, S. Troncoso and E. Rubio _REDCO Mining Consultants Av. La Dehesa 181 of. 208 Lo Barnechea, Santiago, Chile emadariaga@redcoglobal.com_ 

## **ABSTRACT** 

One of the main tasks during the short-term scheduling process is to generate the extraction sequence inside each bench. This sequence represent a feasible mining scenario and when is combined with cut-off grades and mining and processing capacities, constitutes a production schedule that represent the expected operational outcome in terms of tonnages, grades and fine copper production. Normally, this sequence is constructed over a deterministic block model and is focused in to obtain the larger possible amount of copper fines, considering that in a short-term scenario, mining and process capacities are fixed. Moreover, is not unfrequent to see that short-term schedule tries to reach the metal production promised in Budget, absorbing operational delays and miscalculations during the budget scheduling, so the searching for the in-bench sequence that reach the desired metal production left little room to face any kind of variability during the actual mining process since it is already overstressed from the schedule. Despite the expertise of the mine planner, that maybe could reduce to a minimum the chance that operations cannot follow the timing of the mining sequence, the natural uncertainty of the ore body (in terms of grades, hardness and any other relevant variable) still could jeopardize reaching of the desired productive outcomes. 

This work proposes an empiric and practical approach to selec

t a short-term mining sequence balancing the expected metal production and its associated uncertainty, so the mine planner can take a more informed decision about what mining sequence should be follow in order to limit the outcomes variability. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

## **INTRODUCTION** 

The generation of a short term production schedule is subject to the guidelines set out in the strategic long-term planning and budget compliance of operations determined in the medium-term plan, together with the integration of updated information (Newman and Rubio [4]) from the different areas (mine operations, metallurgy, geology, etc.). Current planning practices and performance of manual methodologies to construct extraction sequences (Troncoso [3]) leave little time to the short-term planner to construct the mining sequence in a more robust way analyzing different scenarios varying the in-bench mining sequence. This reduced flexibility normally induces poor operational practices and deviations to achieve a productive target that frequently is higher than actual capacities due to uncertainty (geological, productive, etc.). The proposed methodology in this work aims to expose to the planner multiple mining sequences and their associated copper fine production volatility due to geological uncertainty. Proposed methodology is base on grade simulations of the block model and mining sequences considering in-bench cuts constructed automatically using VMMBOS2. This allows the planner to choose a robust extractive sequence to face geological uncertainty and raises awareness of the volatility that can be materialized when the production plan is being executed, allowing more consistent decision making at the risk level that can be tolerated. 

## **METHODOLOGY** 

This work proposes a methodology that based on several simulations of a block model and generating numerous in-bench mining sequences, allows the mine planner to take a more informed decision about the sequence that should be mined in order to obtain the larger amount of metal production for a determined variability. The methodology is explained below: 

1. Block model simulations: to construct several block models through geostatistical simulations. If simulations are not available, krigged block model could be perturbed around average grades of each block considering the global variability for each ore type, for example. Whilst this is not the best approach, the objective to have multiple block models is better understood considering the following step. 

2. Mining scheduling: for selected statistical simulation scenarios (could be all the simulated scenarios) generate a feasible mining sequence considering in-bench cuts in a block basis. 

   - a. Save the period when each block was mined (Morales and Rubio [1]). 

   - b. Save the destination of each block (Vargas [2]).

3. Metal production histograms: for each mining

schedule generated in the previous point, considering the mining period and the destination of each block, compute the total copper fines produced from every block model realization. - a. Compute the average metal production for each schedule. - b. Compute the standard deviation of metal production for each schedule. 4. Mining sequence selection: to select the desired mining sequence considering a Return vs. variability graph, where return is total average metal production for each schedule and variability is the standard deviation of metal production of each schedule. Considering that this methodology is intended for short term scheduling, it is not necessary to simulate the entire long term model, just the proper boundary for the scope of the planning exercise, the only step that could make this methodology impracticable (in terms of time consumption) with current planning techniques is step 2. Nevertheless, through VMM-BOS2 is it entirely possible to construct several feasible production schedules with an in-bench cuts basis in hours, making this methodology feasible to insert in short-term planning cycles. ## **CASE STUDY** A full scale case study was implemented in order to test the proposed methodology. ## **CONCLUSIONS** 

The main purpose of this work is to propose an alternative methodology to the traditional accepted ones in mining industry, to make explicit that scoping for higher metal production could be associated to variability and productive risk. 

It is recognized that the proposed methodology is more time consuming than actual practices if manual approach is considered to make in-bench cuts, nevertheless, modern planning tools like VMM-BOS2 could support this methodology in adequate timing to deliver on time schedules. Even if  direct result of VMM-BOS2 are not considered to deliver the official Forecast schedule, the resulting mining sequence applying this methodology can be considered as a guideline to construct the official schedule, in order to generate a more robust forecast.

## **ABSTRACT** 

Currently mining is under stress, operational and capital costs are increasing as well as environmental issues have caused a high level of uncertainty for the development of mining in the next years. Traditional mining involves several processes including the removal and extraction of blasted or caved rock, size reduction through comminution and processing of the ore and the subsequent storage of residues on the surface. Leaching involves the recovery of metals, such as copper, from a pregnant leach solution, which is obtained after the contact between the leaching solution and the ore. _In situ_ leaching is the application of leaching solutions to unperturbed or fragmented rock. _In situ_ leaching of unperturbed rock has been successfully applied to the uranium mining industry. In the case of copper, attempts to leach remnants from the caved rock have been reached with relative success. 

This paper aims to illustrate conceptually a new mining method that integrates _in situ_ leaching and conventional underground mining in a novel way. Such a method termed _in-situ_ mining allows for the recovery of metals from deposits at a lower capital and operational cost when compared to traditional mining. In this concept there is technical work to do in the future, mainly regarding the metallurgical and mining process that to establish the fundamentals of _in situ_ mining. This gap is to be filled by the use of experiments to establish a methodology for the application of ISM in the near future. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

272 

## **INTRODUCTION** 

In the near future,  mining will have new challenges to face, being one of the main difficulties not a shortage of mineral resources but a lack of adequate technologies that will allow the recovery of metals from decreasing grade deposits. The decline in average copper grades, the increasing depth of the deposits, the depletion of copper oxides and the increase of energy has caused an overall increase in operational and capital mining costs [1-2].  The increment on costs is causing a review of several projects by the industry with many being not rentable under uncertain market and financial conditions. Today sulfide ores are generally extracted by either pyr

ometallurgical or hydrometallurgical means. The main hydrometallurgical processes are dump, heap and tank leaching, and in a lower proportion, _in situ_ leaching. 

_In situ_ leaching (ISL) considers irrigating an ore deposit with a leaching solution through injection wells. The injected solution flows through the ore through channels, reacting and resulting in the solubilization of certain metals, which creates the pregnant leach solution (PLS). This solution is then sent to the surface by means of recovery wells to be processed. 

In the case of uranium, ISL accounted for 45% of the world´s extraction in 2011 [3]. With regard to copper, the results obtained in the San Manuel and Miami mines in Arizona, USA, showed interesting results [4].  However further investigation is needed in order to determine the conditions under which this method can be successfully applied. 

The main advantages of _in situ_ leaching are [5-7]: 

- Lower grade deposits, isolated ore bodies or deep underground zones may be mined economically 

- No major surface disturbance in terms of open pits, subsidence by underground mining, waste dumps or tailing dams 

- Eliminate noise and dust problems 

- Reduce health and safety risks for workers 

- Does not require material loading and hauling and crushing or milling. 

- Significantly reduces capital costs and operational costs 

- An increase in mineral reserves due to the decrease in the Cutoff Grade 

Despite all the ISL advantages, the major limitations of this technology include [4,7-8]: 

- Require handling large volumes of solution 

- Solutions leaks with environment and economical considerations. 

- Generally lower copper recoveries and in more prolonged periods of time than those anticipated. 

The efficiency of _in situ_ leaching depends on several aspects including rock fragmentation, the usage of heated air or leaching solutions, and the use of procedures to improve the permeability of the leached zone. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

In this article we introduce the term _in situ_ mining that is a combination of _in situ_ leaching and conventional mining. In order to accomplish this goal, experiments will be developed to observe the degree of influence of the three main variables on the copper recovery process.  The three variables to be examined in this preliminary research are; air incorporation, solution heating and the effect of mineral extraction.

This paper presents a study of the cycle times for the operation of autonomous trucks, showing which is the challenge of today´s technology, achieving the system’s operational continuity, maximizing the operational daily hours of autonomous trucks.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

The current autonomous trucks operation started with the tests performed from 2005 to 2006 in Codelco’s Radomiro Tomic Division. The results obtained allowed this technology to go from pilot tests in a special sector of the mine prepared for this operation to an industrial stage, with defined KPIs and an organization willing to consolidate its operation. 

After six years, we can say that today´s technology is validated and has sustainably achieved the expected results in the first stage. 

Today, we are in continuous improvement, in an on-going challenge to find better results. 

One of the advantages of operating with autonomous trucks is that they allow operating more hours per day. To achieve this, we must know, understand, operate, design and plan this technology, incorporating analysis tools, and detecting and managing variability based on KPIs. 

## **What is an Autonomous Operation?** 

It is an integrated open pit mining system, which allows the safe and efficient interaction of traditional manned mining equipment (shovels, graders, dozers, drills, etc.) and a fleet of autonomous 930E4 AT Komatsu trucks. 

For this purpose, it uses a high-speed wireless network, a GPS global positioning system, and control systems on-board the truck. All of this is supported by an organization of operators, maintainers and supervisors, that are duly trained and qualified to manage day-to-day planned goals.

## **CONCLUSIONS** 

There is a high variability in cycle times for a totally autonomous truck, reflecting events that affect the autonomous operational productivity, with a spread of 13.7% above its estimate. This leads to innovate with respect to fixed and variable cycle times and to generate estimators depending on the transport cycle to be developed by the truck. 

Hence, we conclude that the original methodology, introduces a bias in the cycle time estimation and in turn in the autonomous truck time productivity, making it essential to continue executing analyses and studies to minimize bias. 

A variable schedule including stochastic tools may be the solution to minimize that bias. Six Sigma total quality methodologies must be incorporated as tools to make a cause analysis of the variability in fixed time cycle times and that maintain these estimators, in a controlled environment. This allows determining success or events processes that are interconnected and that interact with the truck cycle times, such as delays that are primarily active in the truck travel times and that affect the speed of the truck while it travels, either while decreasing its speed or stopping, hence increasing the transport cycle time.

## **INFLUENCE OF GEOLOGICAL VARIABILITY ON THE DYNAMICAL FEATURES OF ROUGHER TAILING SAMPLES**

## **ABSTRACT** 

The relationship between geological unit characteristics and the rheological behavior of tailings is of great interest due to its impact on thickening, transport and deposition. In order to understand this relationship, it is necessary to study the rheological behavior of tailings produced from ores with known mineralogical characteristics and different combinations of lithology and alterations of the hypogene mineralization zone of a deposit. Two hundred laboratory rougher tailings samples were characterized. Measuring included solids density, particle size distribution and rheograms obtained with a Searle-type coaxial cylinder rheometer. The rheograms were determined at different concentrations of solids and the results were assimilated to the Bingham plastic model that has turned out to be convenient and practical for this type of suspensions. An explicit relationship between different tailings with their own geological properties and rheological characteristics was reached. These results enable us to be provided with more solid design bases for thickening, transport and deposition. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

294 

## **INTRODUCTION** 

Tailings management, mainly thickening, transport and deposition operations, has been widely studied. However, the relationship between these operations and the geology of the ore has only been partially analyzed despite its influence on the sustainable development of the business. 

The complexity and mineralogical variability of a deposit is generally extensive. In order to handle this issue, the deposits are divided into different zones or dominions with similar rock lithologies and alterations. 

This complexity and variability of the deposit has a strong influence on the dynamic behavior of tailings and therefore, quantifying this effect is of utmost importance, both in the design stages and in the operation of the plant. 

In order to study the influence of geological variability of the hypogenous zone of a deposit on the behavior of tailings generated from the processing of its ores, a methodology that includes physical, sedimentological and rheological characterization of a set of rougher tailings samples whose spatial location in the deposit is known has been defined. 

Physical characterization includes determining solids density and particle size distribution. With the sedimentological study it is possible to know the settling behavior of the particles suspended in the liquid. The values obtained are a fundamental variable for determining the thickening area required for concentrating the solids contained in the tailings and recovering the liquid fraction of the slurry in order to return it to the process and reuse it. With the rheological characterization it is possible to determine yield stress and viscosity of the slurry; these results are design parameters for tailings transport lines an

d deposition. 

The objective of this study is to demonstrate that the high variability of a deposit influences tailings behavior, an aspect that may be incorporated into the design of tailings management systems and the planning of the operation to obtain optimum results with it. 

## **MATERIALS AND METHOD** 

The samples dealt with come from the hypogeneous zone of a deposit whose spatial location and NIR mineralogy are known. These samples can be grouped into 10 deposit lithology and alteration sets. The number of samples in each set is proportional to its abundance in the studied deposit. 

The samples were obtained by standard flotation, which included drying. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

295 

Solids density was determined by gravimetry using a Gay-Lussac pycnometer. The particle size distribution curve was obtained by means of a laser analyzer according to standard BS-ISO 13320. 

The settling rate was determined using graduated glass cylinders, recording the interface height throughout time. 

Viscosity (µ) and yield stress (τy) were determined based on rheograms obtained by means of a Searle-type coaxial cylinder rheometer. This equipment allows the slurry to be submitted to shear. Angular velocity (Ω) and torque (T) are measured. To obtain slurry µ and τy values, the T and Ω values obtained undergo ad hoc algorithmic processing, using the RHEOCIPS software developed by the Centro de Investigaciуn de JRI (JRI Research Center). 

A relevant problem in this type of tests is the rapid settling of suspensions containing relatively large particles (around 100 [µm]); to avoid this difficulty, a special probe is used. 

All the settling and rheological tests were conducted using a single dose of flocculant and process water. For convenience, the tests were conducted at pH 10. 

The errors of each of the methods used were determined and validated using specific protocols developed by the Centro de Investigaciуn de JRI (JRI Research Center).

## **GEOLOGY AND ORE DEPOSITS** 

## **Regional Geological Structure and Mineral Deposits** 

The Indochina Peninsula surrounding Laos consists of three small continental blocks (South China, Indochina, and Sibumasu) and fold zones among these blocks (Fig. 2) (Ueno and Hisada, 1999). After the blocks were separated from Gondwana land in the Devonian period to the Permian period, they collided with each other and again accumulated in the Permian period to the Triassic period. The collision between the Indochina block and the Sibumasu block enclosed the Paleo-Tethys Ocean between these blocks and formed the Sukhothai Zone (geologic body originated from the island arc in the Permian period to the Triassic period) and the Inthanon Zone (thrust belt mainly consisting of oceanic rocks originated from Paleo-Tethys) that are considered to be the border of these blocks. The fold zone is regarded an accretionary prism formed through the east facing subduction of the oceanic crust that occurred in the late Triassic period on the west rim of the Indochina block. Igneous activities originated from the subduction resulted in the formation of volcanic rocks and intrusive rocks of calc-alkali rock series. The Loei belt, which covers the South Moune area, has  distribution of I-type granites (quartz-diorite, granodiorite, quartz monzonite, etc.) of calc-alkali rock series in the Permian period to the Triassic period. It is known that there are various types of mineralization relating to these granites, including mineralization of porphyry type, skarn type and epithermal vein type. Moreover, Panjasawatwong et al. (2006) indicate that basic volcanic rocks in the Loei belt may have been formed in the oceanic basin or mature back-arc basin and that there may be volcanogenic massive sulfide deposits.

## **Geology and Ore Deposits of South Moune Area** 

The geology of this area consists of sedimentary rocks and volcanic rocks in the Carboniferous system to the Permian system. These rocks, from lower to upper layer, consist of mudstone and sandstone layer, basalt layer, and mudstone and sandstone layer (l

imestone kept in between), into which small scale granites are intruded. With regard to alternation, a broad range of silicification is observed in the sedimentary rocks. In addition, the X-ray diffraction test of the powder detected smectite in the vicinity of the mineral occurrences and a northwestern part of the South Moune area. Chlorite and sericite were also observed in many samples, indicating weak argillization. ## **Characteristics of Mineralization in the South Moune Area and Guidelines for Exploration** 

The drilling survey resulted in observing that several sites in the Phu Sarana mineral occurrence have a mineralization area of over a 1% copper grade on average. In these mineralized part, chalcopyrite and pyrite were observed being associated with calcite veins and quartz veins and in black mudstone as dissemination minerals (Fig.6). In addition, since pyrite showing framboidal texture was observed, it was thought that the mineralization was associated with organic matter. Considering the copper mineral occurrence of the Phu Sarana, copper mineralization is closely related to the black mudstone and there is a possibility which indicates that the presence of the black mudstone played an important role in forming copper mineralized parts (Ozasa et al., 2012). 

In the future, we will unveil characteristics of copper mineralization in this area by conducting drilling surveys to detail the distribution of black mudstone that is followed by strong copper mineralization and to identify conditions of the mineralization. At the same time, we will seek the presence of ore deposits that can become a development target.

## **ABSTRACT** 

The oxidation of pyrite in the Chinh Bac mine waste dump (Vietnam) leads to the release of heavy metals, salts and acidity. A long-term water and rock sampling campaign of the waste dump and its surrounding open-cast mines was undertaken. The assessed information was used as input data for a geochemical modelling study to predict the pore water evolution and contaminant discharge from the waste dump. These calculations simulated the 1-D reactive transport in the unsaturated zone of the waste dump and considered the following processes: diffusive gas transport, advectivedispersive solute transport, chemical interactions (e.g. sorption, dissolution, precipitation) between dissolved species, primary and secondary mineral phases and the gas phase. The annual rainy and dry seasons were also regarded. This aspect is important for simulating subtropical conditions of NE-Vietnam, where significant seasonal differences regarding the precipitation and percolation is common. As a result of the geochemical calculations, the pore water evolution (and released contaminant loads) into the ground- and surface water was determined and different remediation options (e.g. revegetation) to prevent further acid mine drainage (AMD) generation were suggested.

## **INTRODUCTION** 

The oxidation of sulphide minerals present in rocks or tailings can lead to the generation of acidic, iron and sulphate rich seepage and mine waters (acid mine drainage (AMD) or acid rock drainage (ARD)). Due to the high solubility of various metals under acidic and oxidizing conditions, these waters can have high loads of sulphate and potentially toxic heavy metals. The discharge of the latter into the hydrosphere may lead to the damage of aquatic ecosystems and ground water resources [1]. 

Primary factors which control the generation of contaminated

waters are the quantity as well as the type and reactivity of the sulphide phases present. Furthermore, the availability of oxygen, water and sulphide oxidizing bacteria are important factors for the generation of AMD. Due to its abundance, the oxidation of pyrite (FeS2) plays a key role for the generation of acidic mine waters [2]. 

The acid generation in a waste dump may lead to various consequences which have an impact on the water quality. These include acid induced dissolution of mineral phases, mineral precipitation, ion exchange processes, adsorption and desorption. The acid formed due to the sulphide oxidation can be buffered by reaction with carbonates or other phases such as sheet silicates, iron and aluminium hydroxides. Due to these processes, even at high rates of sulphide oxidation, waters with pH values in the neutral regime may result. 

In this study, the long term pore water evolution and contaminant discharge due to AMD of a Vietnamese hard coal waste dump named Chinh Bac was modelled by the proprietary reactive transport model TAILINGS. In this context, an extensive drilling, field/lab testing and sampling program was designed to acquire representative input data for TAILINGS.

In this section, the basics of the geochemical model which was used to calculate the pore water evolution and contaminant discharge are briefly described. The geochemical model is based on the coupled reactive transport model TAILINGS which was developed by Nitzsche et al. [4]. The software implements the _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 323 principles of reaction kinetics, thermodynamics and transport theory. The following processes are considered in TAILINGS [2]: water flow in variably saturated porous media, diffusive gas transport in partial saturated pore systems, advective-dispersive solute transport, interactions between dissolved species, solid mineral phases and newly formed secondary phases and gaseous components as well as the influence of the rainy season (May - October) and the relatively dry season (November - April) on the percolation rates. The size of the model column is set to 130 m which is assumed to be the approximate thickness of the unsaturated zone based on the observations of the ground water level monitoring. TAILINGS is able to simulate the acid generation due to the oxidation of sulphide minerals, the release of acidity and contaminants from secondary mineral pha

ses (e.g. Jarosite, Melanterite), the neutralization/buffering of acidity due to the dissolution of mineral phases such as carbonates, sheet silicates or iron- and aluminium hydroxides, silicate weathering, generation of dissolved aquatic complexes and their influence on the solubility of the participating species, the mobilization of heavy metals due to the aforementioned processes and their retardation due to sorption and/or precipitation in order to predict the water quality. 

## <u>Water flow</u> 

In TAILINGS, the transient isothermal water flow with uniform density is simulated in a partly saturated porous medium [2]. To describe the underlying processes, the Richards equation [5] was used (not shown). To simultaneously describe the water flow under water saturated and unsaturated conditions, the approach of Celia et al. [6] was used [2]. In the model approach presented in this study, the water flow and solute transport are treated separately. Both systems are coupled in such a way, that at every time step the moisture distribution and the distribution of the Darcy-velocity are calculated which are used as input for the transport model. Here, the finite-element model SWMS_2D is implemented. This model was extended by appropriate routines to describe the gas transport and the relevant geochemical processes [2]. 

## <u>Gas transport</u> 

The sulphide oxidation rate and thus the extent of acid generation are determined by the oxygen transport into the pores. Regarding the oxygen input into dump material or tailings, the processes molecular diffusion and advective transport of solutes are of importance. Especially the diffusive oxygen transport in unsaturated pores is paramount [2]. In order to calculate the oxygen diffusion coefficient, the approach of Rogers & Nielson [7] was chosen (equation not shown). The approach of Rogers & Nielson [7] offers a conservative and realistic basis to describe the oxygen flow through the dump. At the upper cell of the model column, a pressure boundary condition (according to the atmospheric conditions) was set. At the lower cell of the model column, the gas flow was set to 0 due to water saturation [2].

## <u>Integrated approach for the reactive transport modelling</u> 

The calculation of the advective solute transport including geochemical interactions is undertaken with the direct substitution approach [8]. Here, the transport equations and the relevant reaction equations are summarized into one equation per master species and are solved simultaneously [2]. An extensive description of the direct substitution approach can be found in Mayer [9]. 

The coupling of the gas and water transport is done by addition of the model equations for the gas transport and the advective-dispersive transport in the aqueous phase. Kinetic reactions are considered by the reaction term in the transport equation for the dissolved components. Finally, a non-linear system

of differential equations is produced [2] (not shown). 

The conversion of the described system into an algebraic system of equations was done by means of the finite element method. For the linearization of the non-linear algebraic equation system the Newton-Raphson-Method was used. For the iterative solution of the linearized system, the appropriate modules of the SWMS_2D-codes are applied [2]. 

## **Input parameters** 

## <u>Basic geochemical data: Processes, species and mineral phases</u> 

The main geochemical processes which impact the chemical milieu of the dump are the oxidation of sulphide minerals (mainly pyrite) and thus acid generation, carbonate buffering by means of siderite dissolution (FeCO3), buffering due to silicate dissolution, precipitation (and eventually dissolution) of secondary minerals, release of heavy metals due to the aforementioned processes and sorption/retardation of dissolved aquatic species. On the basis of these processes and the available data on the dump composition and seepage water chemistry, the following components and parameters were regarded in the geochemical model: pH, Eh, Ca<sup>2+</sup> , Mg<sup>2+</sup> , Na<sup>+</sup> , K<sup>+</sup> , SO42-, CO32-, Mn2+, Cl-, H4SiO40, Al<sup>3+</sup> , Fe<sup>2+</sup> , Cu<sup>2+</sup> , Ni<sup>2+</sup> , Pb<sup>2+</sup> and Zn<sup>2+</sup> . 

The mineral phases implemented in the model are on the one hand already present in the dump as primary or secondary minerals. On the other hand, phases which may be formed in the long term due to the geochemical processes are also regarded. All mineral phases and their corresponding reaction equations used to describe the mineral dissolution including the equilibrium constants were taken from [10]. 

Certain reactions between the solid and aqueous phases (e.g. dissolution/precipitation of gypsum) considered in the geochemical model are, compared with the timescales of water and gas transport, relatively fast. These reactions are mainly determined by the thermodynamic equilibrium. On the other hand, processes such as 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

325 

pyrite oxidation or the silicate weathering are determined by the reaction kinetics and thus are described here with a complete kinetic approach [2]. 

For those mineral phases for which dissolution was modelled as an equilibrium process, an instantaneous precipitation under equilibrium conditions (that is, when oversaturation is achieved) was permitted in the model. For the other phases, for which dissolution was modelled as kinetically controlled process, the precipitation was disabled since the latter was not considered to be realistic under the pressure and temperature conditions present in the dump. In total, the reactions of 36 mineral phases were considered in the model. Among others, these were Alunite, Anglesite, Azurite, Calcite, Chalkopyrite, Chlorite, CuCO3, Jarosite, Jurbanite, Kaolinite, Montmorillonite, Muscovite, Pyrite, Siderite, Quartz [2

]. 

Reactions between dissolved species, i.e. the formation of aquatic complexes, redox reactions and also reactions with gaseous components were modelled as equilibrium processes [2]. The considered species, the reaction equations and the equilibrium constants were taken from [10]. Due to the space limitation of this article the data cannot be shown. 

## <u>Kinetic parameters</u> 

In order to predict the contaminant discharge of the waste dump, the pyrite oxidation and the buffering of the generated acid through siderite, sheet silicate (Muscovite, Chlorite, Kaolinit, Montmorillonite) and quartz dissolution were modelled as kinetically controlled processes. In order to determine the pyrite oxidation rates by oxygen and dissolved Fe<sup>3+</sup> , respectively, the approach of Williamson & Rimstidt [11] was chosen. The oxidation rates of the other sulphide minerals considered in the model (Chalkopyrite, PbS, NiS) were adjusted to be proportional to the pyrite oxidation rate and were calculated in a similar fashion as the pyrite oxidation rate. Density differences between the different sulphide phases were neglected [2]. For the Chinh Bac waste dump, the pH-dependent silicate and siderite weathering rates were described for quartz, muscovite, chlorite, kaolinite, montmorillonite and siderite. 

## <u>Sorption parameters</u> 

The sorption of heavy metals and other dissolved species was modelled by the surface complexation onto Fe(OH)3. According to Dzombak & Morel [12], weak and strong sorption sites can be distinguished. The reaction equations implemented in the geochemical model and the selectivity constants were taken from Dzombak & Morel [12]. Note, that the sorption reactions of Ca<sup>+2</sup> , Ni<sup>+</sup> , Fe<sup>+2</sup> , Pb<sup>+2</sup> , Cu<sup>+2</sup> , SO4-2, Zn+2 and H+ were regarded. The fraction of binding sites per mole precipitated Fe(OH)3 was constant during a simulation run. Based on Waite et al. [13], the number of weak sorption sites was set to 0.84 mol/molFe(OH)3 and the number of strong sorption sites was set to 0.0021 mol/molFe(OH)3 [2].

## **RESULTS** 

In this section, the concentration profiles of selected solutes in the pore water are presented. Due to space saving reasons, only a very brief insight into the modelling results can be given. 

## <u>Concentration profiles</u> 

Figure 3a exemplary shows the temporal evolution of the sulphate concentration in the seepage water (scenario A, plateaus). The sulphate concentrations in the pore water are generally determined by the elution of the initially present sulphate concentrations and also by the sulphate generation due to pyrite oxidation. As can be seen, the sulphate concentration increases significantly in the first 20 years (red lines in Figure 3a). With the progression of time, the sulphate front is transferred into larger depths. Due to the pyrite oxidation in the upper dump regions, after a about 300 years no sulphate is delivered anymore and the sulphate concentrations sink accordingly in the upper dump section. The calculated pH decreases initially in several m below the dump surface and increases again with increasing simulation duration (Figure 3b). This increase is the result of the buffering due to the (kinetically slow) siderite and sheet silicate (muscovite/chlorite) dissolution. Although the concentrations of the buffering minerals in the dump are significantly above the pyrite content, due to the slow silicate and siderite dissolution AMD generation still takes place. Since the buffering processes become only significant after pyrite is consumed, the pH increases again with time.

The predicted concentrations of the trace metals nickel and lead depend on their release due to pyrite oxidation, the generation or precipitation of secondary minerals, partly pH-dependent sorption processes and the initial pore water concentrations. Furthermore their concentrations are influenced by the percolation rate which controls their elution. Since Fe(OH)3 precipitates only in the very surface near regions of the model, the heavy metals are not retarded due to sorption onto Fe(OH)3. Only the Pb concentration is temporarily limited due the precipitation of Anglesite. ## **CONCLUSIONS** 

A long term water and rock sampling/monitoring campaign of the Chinh Bac waste dump and the circumjacent open cast mines was undertaken. The assessed information used as input data for a reactive transport modelling study in order to predict the contaminant discharge of the waste dump. The geochemical modelling results showed that a long term contaminant discharge from the Chinh Bac dump has to be expected. Contaminant  concentrations (sulphate, heavy metals) will be elevated over several hundred years so that an appropriate remediation of the dump is paramount. Unfortunately, due to the large dimensions of the dump, many reasonable and costefficient remediation options cannot be implemented anymore. As a result of the investigations, it was found that the construction of berms, revegetation, catchment and diversion of dump surface water and water catchment/treatment are feasible options in order to limit the impact of AMD on the environment.

The Kratie North project of the company engaged in exploration for gold from 2008 in the form of a joint venture with JOGMEC, Japan Oil, Gas, and Metals National Corporation. However, JOGMEC withdrew itself from the joint venture in 2010.

## **GEOLOGY AND ORE DEPOSITS** 

## **Regional Geology** 

Figure 2 illustrates a general geological map of Cambodia. The country is located in the southern rim of the Kontum Shield. After the effect of the Indosinian orogeny, the country is classified into the areas of fold belts and the areas of sedimentary rocks overlying these fold belts.  The geology consists of metamorphic rocks, 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

337 

sedimentary rocks, and igneous rocks, the ages of which range from the Precambrian era to the Quaternary period. 

## <u>Metamorphic Rocks, Sedimentary Rocks, and Igneous Rocks</u> 

The distribution of the Precambrian is found in the northeastern and northwestern parts of Cambodia. Most of the geology of these areas are composed of metamorphic rocks such as gneiss. The Indosinian orogeny, consist of sedimentary rocks fo

rmed in the Devonian period through the Triassic period, which are distributed in the peripheral areas of the Precambrian and the Kampot area in southern Cambodia. The Paleozoic rocks of the Non-tectonic Belt consist of mainly limestone and calcareous sedimentary rocks, which are spotted in islets in the central plain of the country.

Figure 2-Regional Geological Map of Cambodia (after Fortaine and Workman, 1978)

The Triassic rocks turn from marine sediments into continental sediments as the ages of the rocks become younger, and is accompanied by rhyolitic volcanic activities in the Middle to Late Triassic. It is also known that many activities of granite occurred in the Late Triassic. 

The Lower Jurassic consists of acidic to intermediate volcaniclastic rocks which are distributed in the western mountains of the country. The main rock type of the Lower Jurassic is terrestrial sedimentary rock ~~s,~~ which is called the "Terrain Rouge," and is widely distributed in the northeastern Cambodia. Small-scale distribution of marine sediments is found along the border with Vietnam. 

The stratum of Upper Jurassic to the Cretaceous, consisting of continental sediments which are called the "upper sandstone bed". The “upper sandstone bed” is found in the area from the northern part to the western mountains of the country and correlated to the Khorat Group in Thailand. The sedimentary rocks of the same age in the eastern Cambodia are known as the "Cato Formation," which gradually turn from conglomerate and sandstone into andesitic lava and tuff. 

The strata of the Paleogene to the Miocene are lacking in the country. The Upper Tertiary forms a large sedimentary basin in the eastern area of the country. The strata consist of mudstone and siltstone lying on top of a well-developed conglomerate bed. The same strat are seemingly distributed in deep underground of the central of the country. It is an old alluvium formed more than 650,000 years ago. 

Plateau basalts of the Pliocene to the Quaternary spread in a broad range. The lithofacies indicate basalt, alkali basalt and high alumina basalt, all of which are tholeiitic. 

The Quaternary is distributed generally in low flatland that ranges from 0 m to 40 m above sea level, especially in the area from the vast central plain to the northern highlands. 

## <u>Intrusive Rocks</u> 

- `・` High alumina granite of the Paleozoic era

Press granite in northern Kampot, which is accompanied by small stocks and volcanic neck, is estimated to have been formed during activities in the early to middle Paleozoic. The rock type is sheared acid biotite granite. 

Bokham granite found in the Se San River Valley in northeastern Cambodia is two mica granite containing garnet. Although the radioactive dating indicated that the granite was formed in the Indosinian orog

eny(227 Ma), the igneous activity is thought to have occurred earlier. 

## `・` Diorite-granodiorites of the Permian and the Triassic 

These granitic rocks dot across northern Cambodia, indicating a range of composition from gabbro to granite, and formed in the later stage of the Indosinian Orogeny. 

## `・` Diorite-granodiorites of the Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous 

Granitic rocks of these periods indicate intermediate to granitic composition, which are distributed in the Mekong River basin and the central part of northern Cambodia. Although the radioactive dating indicates the age of formation from 172 Ma to 67 Ma, the mode is concentrated in a range between 125 Ma and 100 Ma. 

- `・` Intrusive rocks of the Cretaceous-Paleogene 

Intrusive rocks represented by the Cole body and the Nonai body and found in the western part of the central lowland consist of monzonitic biotite granite, younger aplite and microgranite. 

## <u>Past Surveys in the Phnom Basset Area</u> 

Mineral occurrences in the Phnom Basset area have long been known. A report of a Chinese survey team (1975) appeared for the first time in literature. According to the literature, the mineralization of the prospect occurs as quartz veins containing molybdenite, general strike/dip of which is EW/80°S. The quartz veins are generally 5 to 10 m long and 2 to 10 cm wide.  Frequency of veins range from 5 to 8 veins/m in part 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

341 

that follow in the principal joint direction.  The mineralization zone ranges some 80 m in width and more than 800 m in length and elongates in the east-west direction.  The analytical value of quartz veins containing molybdenite indicated 0.14%Mo while that of biotite granite found in the vicinity indicated 0.01%Mo. 

Around 1990, geologists at the Institute of Technology of Cambodia reevaluated the prospect. They revealed that the monzonite formed a zonal structure that indicated ~~s~~ an intrusive dome, which is favorable environment for molybdenum mineralization. Their study indicated that the prospect had the average Mo content of 0.036%Mo and the ore reserve of 10 to 20 million tons when the depth of the ore body was 50m. 

Many study groups have examined the study on this prospect. However, their examinations, indicated that the mineralization in the prospect was too weak and too small to develop. An investment company of Singapore also conducted geochemical survey in December 2005. 

Meanwhile, the Russian survey team who visited Cambodia in the early 1990s recommended the preservation of the prospect to the Cambodian government because the mineralization occurrence is a useful mineral resource for the country. 

## **Surface Exploration** 

In July 2006, Nittetsu Mining concluded a Memorandum of Understanding (hereinafter "MOU") with the MIME on preliminary surveys which is necessary for obtainment of an exploration license under the Law on Management and Exploitation of Mineral Resources of Cambodia. Du

ring the period of the MOU, Nittetsu Mining conducted surface geological survey and geochemical survey in its first exploration and a geophysical survey using induced polarization (IP) method in its second exploration. 

## <u>Surface Geological survey and geochemical survey</u> 

The result of the surface geological survey and geochemical survey in the Phnom Basset area are summarized as follows: 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

342 

The Phnom Basset area constitutes potassium feldspar porphyritic monzonite of the pre-mineralization stage, and monzonite porphyry complex of the mineralization stage which serves as the host rock for the mineralization (Figure 3).The lithofacies of the monzonite porphyry complex are classified into 4 types, i.e., quartz porphyry, monzonite porphyry, porphyritic monzonite and fine grained monzonite. The complex forms a zonal structure with the quartz porphyry at the core. The Phnom Basset area has been known as a molybdenum prospect. But since results of this survey also identified copper mineralization, the prospect is highly likely to be a porphyry molybdenum-copper deposit.Molybdenum-copper mineralization are observed in two types of quartz veins, i.e., veins that contain ~~s~~ chalcopyrite -(bornite)-pyrite accompanying an alteration with secondary biotite and secondary potassium feldspar (vein A) and in veins that contain ~~s~~ molybdenum -pyrite-chalcopyrite (vein B).  These mineralized quartz veins are hosted by quartz porphyry, monzonite porphyry and porphyritic monzonite. Strength of the mineralization is correlated with the frequency of quartz veinlets.  In addition, the frequency of quartz veinlets is correlated with the elevation of outcrops; where the altitude is lower, the mineralization tends to be stronger. Results of the geochemical survey indicate the mineralized zone can be divided into 3 zones, i.e., the low Cu-high Mo zone, medium Cu-low Mo zone, and high Cu-high Mo zone, which in turn indicates that there are different levels of erosion in the complex. Some monzonites that are exposed in the southern part of the survey area has the possibility of underground mineralization.

## <u>Geophysical Survey</u> 

The results of the surface geological survey and the geochemical survey in the Phnom Basset area, indicate the presence of promising porphyry molybdenum-copper mineralization exists in the area and that the mineralization seems to get stronger as the level went down deeper.  Therefore, it is important to understand the characteristics of the mineralization in the depth.  Since the mineralization is characterized by the presence of pyrite in the ore body, IP method is thought to be effective. Nittetsu Mining thus set up 12 survey lines (line length 1200-m each) in the Phnom Basset area to conduct the IP survey. The results are summarized as follows: 

The graniti

c rock is broadly distributed over the Phnom Basset area, and therefore the high resistivity zone appeared widely. In particular, in the western part of the survey area where granitic rock exposes on the surface, a zone of high apparent resistivity zone spreads from the shallow depth. Meanwhile, in the eastern part of the area where the granitic rock ~~e~~ is covered with surface soil and scarcely exposed a zone of

In addition, since the contrast of resistivity is very low between the mineralized zone and the surrounding areas, it seems difficult to find anomalies solely by the analysis of resistivity distribution. The chargeability in the Phnom Basset area is relatively high and a lot of data are over 20mV/V. Generally, a porphyry copper deposit tends to have high chargeability anomaly in a broad area. From geological and geochemical survey, the mineralization of this area is likely to be that of porphyry copper type and the results of the IP survey are in accordance with this (Figure 4). In the Phnom Basset area the monzonite porphyry complex has many veinlets that contains sulfide minerals. It is estimated that the high chargeability is caused by the sulfide in these veinlets. Therefore, it can be assumed that the anomaly zone is characterized by high resistivity and high chargeability.

## **Drilling Surveys** 

As discussed above, the results of the surface exploration in the Phnom Basset area are likely to indicate the presence of ore deposits that are similar to porphyry molybdenum-copper deposits. Thus, based on the IP survey, Nittetsu Mining decided to conduct drillings at the spots where high IP anomalies are obtained in the 2D analysis of IP survey. 

In August 2012, Nittetsu Mining conducted an environmental baseline survey in the Phnom Basset area and its surroundings to know environmental conditions prior to drillings. In October 2012, Nittetsu Mining started drillings (7 ~~-h~~ oles, total length of approximately 2,600 m). 

It was observed that the weak copper and molybdenum mineralization existed from the surface through deep underground. 

## **CONCLUSIONS** 

- (1) The Phnom Basset area has long been known as a molybdenum prospect. The results of the surface exploration revealed that the area has a potential of a copper deposit. 

- (2) Nittetsu Mining Co., Ltd. picked up this area as a promising area for copper deposits and obtained an exploration license in April 2012. 

- (3) The Company conducted drillings at the high IP anomaly spots obtained in the 2D analyses of the IP survey. As a result, weak copper mineralization and molybdenum mineralization were observed in the area from surface through deep underground.
